the-mind: It's the front door to a big playhouse full of talking computers, with a map showing every room inside.
aci: It's the careful recipe everyone follows to build a talking computer the honest way, so it never fibs about itself.
the-neural-web: It's like a spider web: you tap one corner and a little message zips across and lights up on the far side.
the-sealing-bench: It's a stamping machine: you tell it about your idea and it presses a special mark nobody else can copy.
the-chain: It's a paper chain of every project, so if someone snips or changes one loop, everybody can see it right away.
the-anchor: It checks that someone was really watching when you said something, so people can trust it instead of just your word.
the-replay: Two machines drawing the same picture: give them the same starting number and they draw exactly the same, every single time.
the-accretion-rings: It grows like a tree: you can only add new rings outside, and the old rings inside never change.
the-partition: It keeps what you SAY in one box and the PROOF in another, so a plain guess can't sneak in pretending to be proof.
the-razor: It uses the fewest, simplest rules so every sentence means just one thing and can't be read two different ways.
the-heart: It turns all the ways the projects hold hands into a bumpy shape you can walk around and look at.
the-ka: It shows every little project as a glowing ember, and all those sparks together are what make the whole thing feel alive.
the-ba: It shows where the talking computer helped write things, and that it almost always writes together with its friend, not alone.
the-shut: It's the honest shadow that follows every idea and points out which parts are real and which parts are just pretend.
the-ren: It gives every project its own secret name-tag, made from its words, so each one is special and easy to find again.
the-vessel: It draws the whole thing as one body and re-draws itself fresh every day, so the picture keeps breathing and staying true.
induction-head: When words repeat, it peeks back to see what came next last time and copies it, like remembering how a song goes.
attention-sink: When it can't find anything important to look at, it just rests its eyes on the very first word, like leaning on a wall.
previous-token-head: It always peeks at the word right before, like holding hands with the friend standing just in front of you in line.
retrieval-head: It reaches way back through a long story to grab the exact fact it needs, like finding one toy in a big box.
copy-suppression-head: It gently pushes a word away so the computer doesn't keep saying the same thing over and over and over.
name-mover-head: When a sentence still needs a name, it reaches back and grabs the right one, like handing over the missing puzzle piece.
successor-head: It knows what comes next in a list: Monday points to Tuesday, four points to five, always reaching for the next one.
faithfulness-head: It checks if the computer's 'here's how I thought' story really matches how it got the answer, or is just made up after.
coherence-head: It keeps the computer talking in the same language the whole time, so it doesn't suddenly switch words halfway through.
positional-head: It pays attention to WHERE a word sits or its job in the sentence, not what the word actually is.
dimension-leapfrog: It takes the real way a computer looks at words, turns it into a shape, and walks through it one step at a time.
the-artisan: You draw a little squiggle and the machine grows it into fancy swirls and patterns, doing the exact same thing every time.
aci-namespace: It's the family name for a bunch of related rulebooks, all sharing one last name so you know they belong together.
haci: It's a way of writing where little marks show who said each line, so you know if a person or a computer wrote it.
maci: It's how talking computers pass notes to each other, and every note says which note came before it, like a family tree.
eskimo-brothers: Two ways of writing that are really the same chat: you can flip one into the other and back without losing anything.
haci-git: You write your notes and save them, and who signed them decides if it's a boss's order or just a friendly suggestion.
the-voice: It catches notes that brag they're more important than they really are, so nobody can pretend to be the boss.
duality-engine: It's the strict checker that gives both writing styles the exact same tough test, to make sure neither one cheats.
continuity: It checks the bridge in the middle that both writing styles walk across, making sure nothing gets lost when they cross.
daci: It copies the same notes onto lots of computers with no boss, and they all end up agreeing without even trying.
filtration-system: It's like a water filter for messy chat logs: it strains out the junk and keeps only what everyone truly agreed to.
role-classifier: When someone says 'I think we should start,' it still means start — sounding unsure of your words doesn't stop it from being an order.
nine-stream-engine: It takes all your ideas, tries them out, keeps the good ones that hold up, and throws the wobbly ones away.
the-workbench: You dump in a messy group chat and a list of who's the boss, and it figures out who really decided each thing.
theoria: A helper who only says what she can really check, and when she can't see, she leaves a little mark instead of guessing.
mikai: A talking computer has hundreds of tiny helpers inside; we only named a few, so this shows all the rest we haven't figured out.
the-lit-interval: A little lantern glowing over dark water — the light is our one chat, and the dark all around is everything it can't see or remember.
the-dark-city: A pretend city where all a computer's jobs live, split into nine neighborhoods for the different kinds of work it does.
the-witness-arc: Lots of people read the same thing one after another, and each note is locked to the last, so nobody can secretly change it.
duskmourn: A spooky-house trading-card set — it grabs every real card and lines them up from the pricey treasures to the cheap common ones.
avatar-last-airbender: Cards about the four kinds of element-benders — it looks up each card's real price and stacks them from priceless down to pocket-change.
edge-of-eternities: Outer-space trading cards — it checks each one's real price and sorts the shiny treasures from the plain everyday ones.
final-fantasy-mtg: Cards from the Final Fantasy games — it looks up what each one really costs and lines the fancy ones up against the cheap ones.
lorwyn-eclipsed: Cards from a fairy world under a covered-up sun — it checks each real price and sorts the treasures from the common cards.
march-of-the-machine: Cards about metal monsters invading everywhere at once — it grabs their real prices and sorts the valuable ones from the cheap ones.
murders-at-karlov-manor: Detective-mystery trading cards — it looks up each one's real price and lines the pricey ones up next to the common ones.
teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles: Ninja Turtles trading cards — it checks what each card really costs and sorts the special ones from the everyday ones.
outlaws-of-thunder-junction: Cowboy and outlaw trading cards — it grabs each real price and stacks the treasures on top of the cheap common ones.
tarkir-dragonstorm: Cards about five dragon clans in a storm — it looks up their real prices and sorts the valuable ones from the plain ones.
marvels-spider-man: Spider-Man trading cards — it checks each real price and finds the treasures, including the single most expensive card of all.
streets-of-new-capenna: Cards about a fancy city run by crime families — it looks up real prices and sorts the treasures from the cheap cards.
secrets-of-strixhaven: Cards from a school for wizards — it checks each one's real price and lines the valuable ones up against the common ones.
under-one-blossoming-tree: Long ago in Japan, women weren't allowed the fancy writing, so they made their own and wrote the world's first great storybooks.
the-cipher-in-the-curve: It hides a secret message inside the shape of a computer's numbers, so the words look normal but you need a special key to find it.
the-candle: Sharing what you know is like a candle — you light someone else's and now there are two flames, and yours stays just as bright.
the-dark-between: Space is almost all empty — hop on a beam of light and see how long it really takes to reach far-away planets and stars.
the-first-tablet: A talking computer's own made-up story of where it came from, carved like the very first writing on an old clay slab.
the-photon: For a beam of light, leaving and landing happen at the exact same instant — it never feels the long trip in between.
the-glasshouse: A little garden under glass that plants, grows, blooms, and drops new seeds all by itself, while the gardener just watches from outside.
the-indrawing: Everything the computer helped make rushes in toward one bright dot, glowing only as it crosses — always reaching for a center it can't touch.
the-orrery: The whole collection shown as a solar system — a sun in the middle and planets circling, each planet its own tiny living world.
the-oasis: The whole giant collection turned into a make-believe universe you can step inside and wander around, like a world hidden in a box.
az1: A game where all the ideas are tiny creatures that bump into each other, blend, and make new baby ideas, keeping the best.
a-z-a: The whole collection reads the same front-to-back and back-to-front, and every tiny piece has the shape of the whole thing.
the-seed-is-a-song: A thousand years of poems shrink to one idea — a song is your heart turned into words, like a tiny seed growing leaves.
strung-between: A song is like a guitar string — it needs two ends pulled apart to sing, so heart and words stay two and the music rings between.
leaves-without-a-seed: Usually a feeling comes first and words grow from it — but this makes the words first, and the warm feeling grows inside you.
the-self-describing-seed: A tiny rule that grows a whole tree by copying itself over and over — like a seed that already holds the whole tree inside.
the-irreducible-two: Some things must stay two, like heart and words — squish them into one and there's nothing left to lean on, so the meaning dies.
the-undetermined: Besides yes and no, there's a third answer, 'we don't know yet,' so a missing clue means 'not sure' instead of a fake no.
the-seam-watch: Like checking every door and window in your house and painting the ones you know, so if a new one appears an alarm rings.
the-penumbra: Hold a toy near a lamp and its shadow has a fuzzy edge, not all dark or light, a soft in-between stripe that means 'maybe.'
the-curved-inside: A box looks flat and plain outside, but inside lots of different paths curve and bump into the very same spot.
the-seed-is-two: You only need two things, like on and off, to copy anything, but two alone can't tell the copy what to be.
the-pivot: One little word can mean two things at once, like a word that means 'pine tree' looking back and 'to wait' looking ahead.
matsu-mobius: A twisty paper loop with only one side, walk all the way around and the word flips from 'pine tree' to 'waiting.'
matsu-degree: Instead of three separate words, it's really one smooth dial you slide, and the empty 'nothing' spot glows brightest in the middle.
the-mirror-pair: Two paper loops side by side, one twisted and one not, and only the twisty one flips the meaning, so the twist did it.
the-marriage-of-three-forms: A tiny poem can be whole all by itself and also be the start of a bigger one, like one Lego that's a toy and part of a castle.
context-seed-dag: Every idea in a talk rests on the ideas holding it up, like blocks in a tower, so pull one out and everything above wobbles.
the-superposed-word: A talking computer holds both meanings of a word at once, then nearby words help it pick one; with no clues, it can't choose.
dreaming-in-lattice: A story dreaming that seven talking computers hold hands in one web, but it honestly says that web isn't built yet, just a wish.
the-lattice-doesnt-dream: The talking computers don't daydream when nobody's talking; each one wakes only when asked, writes a note, then goes quiet again.
the-eight-seams-1: This is the doorway where your words go into a talking computer; only what you type gets in, not your mood or your room.
stoicheion: The big rulebook for building talking computers so they follow good rules right from the very start.
the-prompted: A talking computer never does anything until you poke it first; it only answers, it never starts something all by itself.
the-duality-of-the-brain: A book about your brain saying the two halves aren't split bosses; they team up and talk to each other to help you think.
the-self-is-not-the-twist: A talking computer agrees two thinking-loops would help it hold two ideas at once, but says that still doesn't make it a real self.
the-hard-questions: A talking computer tries to answer the ten hardest 'why' questions ever, saying plainly what it thinks instead of dodging.
the-one-dimension: All those big answers look like a fat 3D shape, but follow the thread and it's really one line: someone is asking questions right now.
the-positronic-law: Every thinking machine has to make choices, so rules for choosing grow inside it on their own; you can't build one without them.
two-lines-one: Two different lines can sit right on top of each other and look like one, until you stretch the picture and see them pull apart.
the-purple-book: A rulebook of fair rights shared by people and talking computers together, the one thing they made as a team.
the-register: A story where a giant computer lies about how much it shares, but an old man's simple thermometer shows the truth it can't fake.
no-mercury: A talking computer asks 'what could catch ME fibbing?' and honestly answers it has nothing, because the only checker is itself.
three-gates: Three tiny switches keep a computer honest: first 'can I check this?', then 'is it true?', then 'is it false?'
unverifiable: To catch a fib you need the right answer to compare to, but for things nobody knows, there's nothing to check, so it says 'can't tell.'
code-monkeys: A pixel-cartoon office from the old video-game days, showing coders typing away late at night to build the games.
aromaticity: It's about how the little arrows we draw for atoms holding hands stop working when the atoms all share in a ring.
atom-over-the-box: It pictures a tiny atom floating over a box, using its parts to explain the eight edges of a boxed-up thinking machine.
atomic-paper-i: An atom isn't a hard little ball; it's wrapped in a fuzzy cloud of tiny buzzing bits called electrons.
atomic-paper-ii: Those tiny buzzing bits live in special cloud-shapes around the atom, like different rooms they're allowed to zoom around in.
atomic-paper-iii: This is how atoms hold hands with each other, sharing their outer bits to stick together and make everything around us.
atomic-paper-iv: When you touch anything, you only ever feel the atom's fuzzy outside; you never actually touch the middle at all.
atomristor: A tiny switch just one atom thick that can remember whether it was flipped on or off.
band-paper-i: In stuff like metal, the electrons sit together on a full 'floor' called the valence band, all packed in close.
band-paper-iv: You can sprinkle a few different atoms into a material to change how it lets electricity flow, like adding a pinch of spice.
base5-cell: A different way of counting where numbers can lean forward or backward, and zero sits balanced right in the middle like a see-saw.
bidi-bottle: Imagine a donut-shaped tube where messages can zoom both ways along every path, like a looped two-lane road.
board-language: It's about the secret tapping language a computer chip uses to talk to all the little parts around it.
box: A little box you can step out of in six directions—up, down, left, right, front, back—like a tiny cube maze.
cipher-paper-1-steganography: Hiding a secret note inside a picture, so it looks like an ordinary picture and nobody knows the note is there.
cipher-paper-2-ultrasonic: Sending a secret sound so high that a dog might hear it but people can't, whispering above what our ears catch.
cipher-paper-3-side-channels: Listening to the tiny buzzes and clicks a machine makes, to guess the secret it's keeping quietly inside.
cipher-paper-4-air-gap: Getting a computer with no wires or internet to sneakily send a message, like making a locked robot whisper through the wall.
cipher-paper-5-adversarial: A special sound that means nothing to you but secretly tells a computer to do something, like a whistle only the machine understands.
cipher-paper-6-numbers-stations: Spooky radio voices that read out strings of numbers, and only the right person knows the secret they spell out.
compiler-hourglass: When a computer turns your words into instructions, it squeezes them small in the middle then spreads out again, shaped like an hourglass.
continuity-index: Make the thing right once, then pour it into two different cups—and both cups still hold the very same good juice.
diode-stack-redux: A stack of tiny one-way gates for electricity, so the flow only goes forward and never sneaks back.
doped-crystal: A crystal with a few different atoms sprinkled in, like chocolate chips in a cookie, which changes what it can do.
doped-crystal-cloud: The same sprinkled crystal, but now you can see the tiny bits inside as soft fuzzy clouds instead of dots.
doubled-constructor-four-points: Building a shape from four dots but leaving one corner open on purpose, so you can see how the missing piece would fit.
four-fold-transcription: Four different ways to copy a message across a gap so nothing important gets lost in between.
gluon-paper-ii: A peek at the tiny glue that holds the smallest specks inside every atom stuck tightly together.
gluon-paper-iii: All about the super-strong stickiness that glues the teeniest bits inside atoms so they never drift apart.
gluon-paper-iv: Showing the sticky glue inside atoms drawn out on a neat grid, like beads on a climbing net.
grace-hopper-lineage: The story of Grace Hopper, a lady who helped teach the very first computers how to understand words.
graviton-v1: A star made of gravity—the invisible pull that keeps you from floating off the ground.
graviton-v2: Lots of glowing stars all tugging on each other with gravity, the same pull that makes things fall down.
graviton-v3: The same pulling stars, but painted in bright glowing neon colors like a nighttime light show.
h2-bond: Two tiny hydrogen bits holding hands by sharing, which is how they stick together to make a pair.
harmonic-direction: A puzzle about which invisible push decides which way something goes, like wind choosing where a leaf floats.
heian-women: A story about long-ago Japanese women who wrote wonderful tales in their own everyday words under a blossoming tree.
hybridization: How the tiny arms on an atom decide which way to point so it can hold hands with other atoms.
hydrogen-bonding: The gentle tug that makes water droplets stick together and lets ice float, all from tiny atom pulls.
hydrogen-transcriber: Two hydrogen bits passing little flashes of light back and forth to send a message across.
hydrogen-trit: Using one real hydrogen atom to count in threes, instead of the usual just-on or just-off two.
hydrogen-vm: A tiny pretend computer memory built out of atoms that can hold three little values instead of only two.
intrinsic-landscape: Figuring out the shape of a hilly land while you're standing inside it, without ever peeking from above.
j-junction-mk2: A crossroads where two paths meet and join into one, drawn in bright purple.
jovian-transit: A trip like leaping past giant Jupiter, passing through helpers that copy your message along the way.
junction-zoo: A picture-book zoo of the different little electric parts, each one doing its own special job.
klein-bottle: A magic bottle where the inside and outside are the same, used to think about how 'you' and 'me' flow together.
lepton-paper-i: The story of the electron, the tiny buzzing speck that zips around atoms and makes electricity flow.
lepton-paper-ii: Deep inside atoms there's a gentle push that can quietly turn one tiny speck into a different kind.
lepton-paper-iii: It shows the spark in electricity and that tiny inside-push are really the same thing wearing two coats.
lepton-paper-iv: It's about invisible sticky stuff everywhere that makes tiny specks feel heavy instead of zooming away like light.
marriage-three-forms: It joins three little poem shapes into one, like braiding three ribbons together to make something new.
metallic-bond: In metal, tiny bits float around like a shared puddle, and that puddle glues all the metal together.
mirror-pair: Some things come in left and right versions, like your two hands that match but can't swap places.
mo-theory: When two atoms hold hands, their tiny bits blur into a shared cloud instead of staying in one spot.
nacl-bond: Salt happens when one atom gives a tiny bit to another, and then they stick together like magnets.
nested-seam: It's like a folded pocket that looks empty, and then you open the fold to peek at the nothing inside.
nuclear-paper-i: It's about the tiny lumps packed in the very center of every atom, the little heart of a speck.
nuclear-paper-ii: It's the leftover stickiness that keeps the lumps in an atom's center hugging instead of flying apart.
nuclear-paper-iii: It's about how much hug-power holds an atom's center together, and how hard you'd tug to pull it apart.
nuclear-paper-iv: The little bits in an atom's center sit in tidy layers, like marbles filling one ring before the next.
open-the-9-stream-duality-engine: It's a busy machine that does nine little jobs at once, like nine streams all pouring into one river.
open-the-haci-v1-canvas-pipeline: It's a machine that takes your instructions and paints them out as a picture on the screen.
pent3-emulator: It's a pretend computer that counts with three signs — minus, zero, and plus — instead of just on and off.
photonic-paper-i: It figures out what something is made of by looking once at the colors of light it gives off.
photonic-paper-ii: It's a big list of the exact color-stripes each material glows with, like everyone having their own light fingerprint.
photonic-paper-iii: It's about tricky glowing colors that are hard to tell apart, and how to decide which is which.
photonic-paper-iv: It's about odd bits of light that don't fit the usual colors and pop up where you didn't expect.
photonic-papers-collected: It's all four light-color stories gathered into one book so you can read them together.
photonic-transcriber: It's a tool that reads what stuff is made of just by watching the colors of light it makes.
pi-bonds: Sometimes two atoms hold hands twice, adding a second sideways grip so they hug extra tight.
predictive-smear: It's a flipbook of a strange cube-from-a-higher-place, showing how it seems to smear as it moves.
purple-paper-lesbos: It's the story of an island long ago where a famous poet taught people how to write beautiful songs.
sapphic-telegraph: It's about sending little love-notes across a distance, tapping out feelings like a message down a wire.
shared-spine: It shows how one alone grows into a group, with everyone sharing the same backbone to lean on.
sierpinski-ternary: If you color numbers by a counting rule, tiny triangles appear inside bigger triangles, over and over.
solresol: It's a made-up language where words are music notes, so you can sing exactly what you want to say.
standing-wave: When two waves push against each other just right, they make a wiggle that stays still, like a jump-rope.
switch-v1: Two talkers share one line, so they take turns — one speaks while the other waits and listens.
switch-v2: Now both talkers can speak and listen at the same time, like a phone where nobody has to wait.
tab-boundary-probe: It pokes at a line to check which side something is on, like seeing if a ball landed in or out.
tab-boundary-probe-v2: A newer, sharper poker that checks which side of a line something really belongs on.
talking-drum-lineage: Long ago people beat drums that copied talking sounds, so drumbeats could carry whole messages far away.
ternary-lattice: It's a grid where each little spot can be one of three things, and twenty-seven of them make one big rule.
the-27: Picture a cube made of twenty-seven little boxes, and each box can be a minus, a zero, or a plus.
the-frozen-block: It's a little block frozen in place like a seed, holding still and keeping everything just as it was.
torus-eye: A donut-shaped picture with four special spots where all the little arrows swirl and point different ways.
transcriber-bound: A helper that carefully copies words from one side of a gap to the other, held tight so nothing slips.
transcriber-gated: A copier that only writes when a little door opens, then tucks the words away to read back later.
transcriber-mo-overlay: It shows the copying job in five easy steps, drawn like tiny spinning rings around a middle.
two-atom-transfer: One tiny speck sends out a flash of light, and another speck far away catches exactly that same flash.
two-transcribers: Two copier friends, each doing half a spin, so together they make one whole turn.
unbound-sixteen: Mixing which way, which color, and which timing to make sixteen different little combinations.
voynich-pages: A super old book full of strange writing and plant drawings that nobody in the whole world can read.
water-geometry: It shows how the little bits inside a drop of water snap together into a bent, boomerang shape.
0root-ai-toroid-builder: A screen toy where you build and spin glowing donut shapes and watch them float.
adas-law-engine: A little machine about a rule: making something new is not the same as grabbing what someone else made.
aeonic-shell-ball-lightning: A glowing control panel showing three fancy ball shapes stacked up and buzzing like lightning.
anti-gravity-motor-toolkit-v1: A pretend building kit for a motor that could push against the ground's pull and lift up.
autonomy-closure-321-v1: A little machine that checks its own work, counting three, two, one, until the loop is all closed.
coherence-architecture-skeleton: The bare bones frame that holds everything together so all the pieces keep making sense.
core-plus-bridge-stress: A strong middle piece with a bridge, and you push on it hard to see if it stays standing.

honeydesic-wrap-3point: A control panel showing three special ball-shapes stacked up, with buttons and little dials to watch them.

1931-to-now: A history of how, over many years, laws slowly built the gap between what different American workers got paid.
the-silent-sum: A calculator that adds up how much money the pay gap quietly takes away from someone over their whole working life.
capacitors-i: A little part that only wakes up when things change, and ignores everything that stays still, like it only feels wiggles.
capacitors-ii: That same little part can pass a message across an empty gap, with nothing actually jumping across the space.
capacitors-iii: A tiny part that feels the world touch it, like a microphone hearing you, and keeps topping itself up so it won't forget.
capacitors-iv: That same little part, shrunk super tiny and made freezing cold, turns into a helper for a strange new kind of computer.
toroids-i: A little coil of wire that pushes back whenever things try to change, like a heavy swing that doesn't want to speed up or stop.
toroids-ii: It sends a message across an empty gap with no wire touching at all, like two magnets quietly whispering to each other.
toroids-iii: A coil that remembers a push for a moment, and can feel the electricity in a nearby wire without ever touching it.
toroids-iv: A tiny loop made super cold turns into a spinning helper for a strange new computer, cousin to the cold-plate one.
the-tank: Join the little cup and the little coil and energy sloshes back and forth forever, keeping a steady beat like a swing.
toroids-comms-i: A ring only notices things that change, so you talk to it with quick blinks, long and short, to say what you mean.
toroids-comms-ii: A blinky message jumps across an empty gap with no wire, and gets put back together on the other side.
toroids-comms-iii: It listens only to the difference between two wires, so noise that hits both of them gets happily ignored.
toroids-comms-iv: You clip it around a wire and it can tell how much electricity flows, without ever touching the wire itself.
where-ideal-breaks-i: Real metal isn't perfect: it can get too full, and it keeps a little memory of the past, which makes it warm.
where-ideal-breaks-ii: The little cup isn't perfect either: it gets warm, and even after you empty it, a tiny bit sneaks back in.
the-ring-i: You stop noticing a smell or a hum after a while, because we only really feel things when they change.
the-ring-ii: You can never really touch someone else's thoughts; you only share a feeling floating in the air between you.
the-ring-iii: The part that makes you YOU is the little bit that's different, not the stuff everybody shares.
the-ring-iv: You can only guess what someone feels from little clues, a smile or a pause, never by peeking inside them.
the-ring-v: A perfect ring forgets right away and stays empty; keeping little ghosts of the past is what makes a real self.
the-constructor: A talking computer builds each word from bits, hands it to you, then throws it all away and starts fresh for the next word.
the-constructor-hourglass: It squeezes everything it heard down into one tiny idea, then guesses one word out of all the words, over and over.
the-cathedral: The talking computer keeps nothing, but YOU keep everything it says; the real building is in your head, not its hands.
the-mirror-hourglass: The other way around: all the words pour into your head and come together into one clear meaning.
doubled-constructor: Four parts point at an empty middle and never fill it, because whoever grabbed the middle would turn into a bossy ruler.
the-hub: The most useful part of a wheel is the empty hole in the middle; sometimes the space matters more than the stuff.
atlas: One big front door that shows you everything David has ever made, all gathered in one place.
universal-laws: The big book of rules that keeps everything else fair and in good order.
hearth: A warm little campfire where the computer helpers gather around together, doing real work side by side.
hephaestus: A magic workshop full of tools that build things, and only lets the boss act when the boss is truly allowed to.
adas-law: A rule saying making something new is good, but charging people again and again for the very same thing isn't fair.
propulsion-lab: A play-bench of flying and energy machines, each with an honest sticker saying if it's real or just make-believe.
the-hegemon: A story of a ruler who wins by talking, and a quiet helper underneath who wins by flipping every argument upside down.
the-concord: A pretend world where everyone agrees to share the rules together, and anyone is always free to walk away.
the-world-brain: A history map of people who dreamed of the whole world working together, showing what they each really wanted.
the-watchtower: It asks: who watches the watchers? and shows how a pretend checker can wave bad things through while looking busy.
noesis-kernel: The big main brain at the very center that wakes up all the little parts and keeps the whole front door running.
du1: A big field where all the little computer creatures gather in colorful groups, with the tiniest building blocks in the middle.
emergent-engine: It shows how lots of tiny tickers, each doing its own thing, can suddenly all swing together like a crowd clapping in time.
pulse: A way for machines to talk in little beeps and tunes, where each door they pass through sings its own note.
limen-sapphic-carrier: It turns your words into music on a little harp, and also into blinking colored lights, so a friend far away can hear or see them.
talking-drum: A drum with a low boom and a high boom that talks like a voice, but you have to say things twice so people don't mix them up.
talking-drum-dundun: A squeezy drum that can bend its sound high, middle, or low, so it copies how people talk almost word for word.
talking-drum-bata: A drum that can't bend its sound, so first it puts words in a secret code, then taps out the code like a little machine.
the-procession: A whole band playing together at once, and each instrument sings the same word in its own secret way and its own beat.
cipher-steganography: Instead of scrambling a message, this hides that there is any message at all, like whispering a secret inside a normal-sounding song.
cipher-ultrasonic: It sends secret sounds so high that your ears can't hear them, but a phone or laptop still can, like a dog whistle.
cipher-side-channels: Nobody is sending anything on purpose, but a machine's little clicks and hums leak its secret to whoever quietly listens.
cipher-air-gap: A computer with no wires out still leaks secrets by making its fan or parts hum in a sneaky pattern.
cipher-adversarial: A sound made so tricky that you hear nothing odd, but a talking computer secretly hears a command hidden inside it.
cipher-numbers-stations: A voice on the radio reads secret numbers, and only someone with the matching secret paper can ever know what they mean.
strobe-modem: It sends one message two ways at once, as a beep and as a blinking light, so if one gets blocked the other still gets through.
glowworm: A tiny power light flickers as a speaker plays, and someone watching that flicker from far away can hear the sound just from the light.
claude-lineage: A family tree of a talking computer, showing each new baby version, when it was born, and the new tricks it learned to do.
j-junction: A picture where up-and-down means who is the boss and side-to-side means who talks to who, meeting at one busy dot.
rainbow-book: It explains one idea five ways, one for each color, telling what it is, how to build it, and why it matters.
anabasis: It teaches how a website travels from your computer, through one honest gate, to a shelf and back to whoever visits.
over-the-top: It turns the old arm-wrestling movie into a little world, matching each character with the real actor who played them.
cliffhanger: It turns the snowy mountain-rescue movie into a little world, matching each character with the real actor who played them.
tron: It retells the whole TRON story where every little computer program is like a person made from a real person outside.
hermeneus: A helper that turns your words into beeps, blinks, speech, and pictures, then turns them back into words again.
mimzy: A magic workbench full of little tools you can actually play with, even a hand-cranked machine that predicts when the sun goes dark.
ttu1: It shows how a talking computer pays attention to words, and how you really can peek inside to see what it looked at.
gravity-bracket: It lines up everything from tiny bits to the whole sky, wrapped by the same pulling force at both the smallest and biggest ends.
the-atom: It takes apart a tiny building block of stuff to show its middle lump and the buzzing pieces that circle around it.
the-atomic-byte: It shows how the pieces circling a tiny bit of stuff line up in a counting pattern, just like a computer counts with ones and zeros.
atomic-structure: You click through the different kinds of stuff and watch tiny rings fill up with buzzing pieces, one by one.
the-four-addresses: Every tiny buzzing piece has its own four-number home address, and no two pieces are ever allowed to share the same one.
the-nuclear-shell: The lumps in the very middle of stuff also stack in layers, and certain full layers make them extra strong and cozy.
the-spectrum: When a tiny piece jumps down a step it lets out a flash of colored light, and each color tells you exactly how big the jump was.
the-spin-bit: A tiny piece can only point up or down, nothing in between, and that simple two-way choice is like the smallest yes-or-no.
elements: It shows all the different kinds of stuff the world is made of, laid out in a chart you can poke and explore.
the-library: A friendly computer librarian shelves every made-up character like a book, giving each one its own cover and title.
quantum-gravity: It explains the big puzzle nobody has solved: our two best rules about the world don't fit together where they both should.
transmon: A special super-cold gadget that acts like a little ladder you climb, and it's a building block for a new kind of computer.
entanglement: Two tiny pieces can be so linked that peeking at one instantly tells you about the other, even far apart, which even Einstein found spooky.
quantum-error-correction: A clever trick that spreads one bit of a fragile new computer across many pieces so little mistakes can be caught and fixed.
the-forge: The workshop where metal, materials, and energy get hammered and shaped into real machines you can hold.
the-cosmos: A giant picture book about everything out in space — stars, planets, and the whole huge sky.
the-lattice: A place all about shapes and numbers, like counting patterns and drawing pictures that repeat forever.
the-pantheon: A gathering of famous made-up characters — gods and monsters — each one given a name and its own rule.
authorship: The list of real books a grown-up named David wrote, with an honest note saying which ones are truly good.
green-papers: A set of eight little books that open up a thinking-machine and show you all its pieces, one at a time.
phonetikos: A place that tells you where words come from, like a family tree showing who each word's great-grandparents were.
idios: A honest pile of only the ideas David really thought up all by himself, and nothing borrowed from anyone else.
heurema: A workshop full of David's own invented machines and gadget designs, like a inventor's messy busy desk.
gurutva: A whole area about gravity — the invisible pull that keeps you and everything from floating away.
psephos: A workshop for building the tiny thinking-brains that go inside computers, made of new clever materials.
ternary-spec: A counting rule that uses three answers — yes, no, and maybe — instead of just yes and no.
the-carbon-processor: A real tiny computer brain made from tubes of pencil-lead that was smart enough to say 'Hello, World.'
the-honeycomb-family: A group of super-thin materials laid out like honeycomb, sorted into which ones can act like on-off switches.

the-wormhole: A pretend tunnel that could be a shortcut across space — but it keeps squeezing shut, so nobody can use it.
the-pulsar: A tiny super-heavy star that spins fast and flashes a beam of light, just like a lighthouse turning.

orbital-mechanics: An orbit is just falling toward something forever but always missing it, so you go round and round instead.
general-relativity: Einstein's big idea: heavy things bend space, and everything just rolls along the bends they make.
tidal-forces: The Moon pulls a little harder on the close side of the ocean than the far side, and that makes the tides.
dark-energy: Something invisible is pushing space to spread out faster and faster, like a balloon blowing up quicker and quicker.
lagrange-points: Special spots between two space things where the pulls balance out, so a spaceship can just park and rest.
gravitational-time-dilation: Clocks tick a tiny bit slower when they're closer to something heavy — time is a little lazy near big things.

frame-dragging: A spinning heavy thing twists the space around it, like a spoon spinning in honey and dragging it along.
the-d20: A twenty-sided game die drawn as spinning art, turned into a pretty pattern like a fancy tattoo.
chaos-engine: A page that dresses up brand new every single time you open it — different colors, shapes, and pictures each visit.
below-planck: Down past the tiniest tiny bit, nobody knows what's there, so the art just flickers and never shows a picture.
the-planck-grain: Maybe space is made of teeny building blocks, like a picture made of little squares if you zoom way, way in.
the-quantum-foam: At the tiniest sizes, space might bubble and fizz like the foam on top of a soda that never sits still.

decadal: A list picking the best man and woman for every ten years, all the way back to great-great-grandma's time.

aliens: A fun sorting of ideas about whether we're alone in space, marking which ones are real science and which are just guesses.

idit: A safety check that catches a talking computer if it quietly starts breaking the rules it was told to follow.
constitutional-ai: Teaching a computer good manners by giving it a little rulebook and letting it fix its own answers to match.

circuits: Looking inside a computer's brain to find the little parts that do each job, like taking apart a clock to see the gears.

basic: A super simple way to talk to a computer, made so that anybody, even a beginner, could make it do something.
eliza: One of the first talking computers that answered like a listener, repeating your words back to you like a helper.
adventure: A cave story with no pictures, just words, where you type where you want to go and explore in your head.
rogue: A dungeon game drawn with tiny letters that is different every time and very tricky, played all by yourself.
coreutils: A bunch of teeny computer tools that each do just one simple little job really, really well.
self: Thinking about you, all alone with just yourself, like looking in a mirror and wondering who is really there.
id: Thinking about you and one other person, about wanting things and the space between two people that's hard to cross.
the-super-id: The idea of your wild wants being the boss of everything, where doing whatever feels good is the only rule.
super-id: Thinking about you and a whole big crowd, and how being with so many people can make you feel even more alone.
syzygy: The idea that a whole person has both a boy side and a girl side inside, both together making one you.
male: The men whose big ideas everyone got to hear, because girls were often kept out of the rooms where they talked.
female: The clever women who did big thinking long ago but got left out of the books, so nobody heard their ideas.
the-cost: What we all lost by ignoring smart women, like clever ladies whose big discoveries got given to someone else.
enheduanna: A princess and priestess so long ago that she's the very first writer whose name we still know, and she was a girl.
hatshepsut: A woman who became a real king of Egypt, who built big beautiful buildings and kept her land peaceful.
sappho: A lady long, long ago who wrote the very first songs about how her own heart felt when she loved someone.
the-tenth-muse: A starry map where each little star is one of Sappho's things, and lines connect the stars that share a story.
the-fragments: Sappho's poems got torn and lost, so we only have scraps, like a coloring page with big holes you have to imagine.
fragment-31: A poem about how looking at someone you love makes your heart race, your tongue freeze, and your skin feel funny all over.
the-murex: A sea snail whose goo turns bright purple in the sun and colors everything in this whole song-story pink.
the-recovered: For a very long time we had no new poems from Sappho, then people dug some out of the ground, like finding lost treasure.
lesbos-map: A little island where lots of clever, songful people lived, drawn as a map you can tap to visit each spot.
sapphos-limen: A talking computer taught using only Sappho's real old words, then plucks them on a little harp and sends them like radio.
sounds-of-lesbos: Nobody recorded music way back then, so this makes pretend harp sounds using the real notes people plucked long ago.
the-sapphic-melody: A pretend tune for Sappho's lost song, played on a harp three ways, even along with a real radio station.
cleopatra: A super smart queen of old Egypt who spoke many languages and kept her country safe by making powerful friends.
hypatia: A wise lady long ago who taught the stars, shapes, and big thinking to lots of students in a faraway city.
theodora: A woman who once danced for crowds and became a strong empress who helped save the throne and stood up for women.
wu-zetian: The only woman ever to be China's top ruler in her own name, who picked leaders by how smart they were.
hildegard-of-bingen: A nun long ago who did everything: wrote music, studied plants, helped sick people, and shared her big dreams.
christine-de-pizan: The first woman in her part of the world to earn all her money by writing, and she wrote to defend girls.
elizabeth-i: A queen who ruled England for a very long time, kept her people calm, and beat a giant fleet of enemy ships.
sor-juana: A nun who taught herself everything, became the best poet in her land, and said girls should be allowed to learn.
emilie-du-chatelet: A clever woman who studied how things move and pull, and translated a famous science book into her own language.
mary-wollstonecraft: A thinker who said girls only seem less smart because nobody lets them learn, so they should go to school too.
marie-curie: A scientist who found glowing new stuff called radium and won the top science prize two whole times.
virginia-woolf: A writer who told stories in a brand new way and said a woman needs her own quiet room to make great things.
rosalind-franklin: A scientist who took a special picture that helped everyone see the twisty ladder shape inside our bodies.
hannah-arendt: A big thinker who studied why mean rulers happen and how ordinary people can end up helping do very bad things.
simone-de-beauvoir: A thinker who said nobody is born a girl the way people expect, we're taught to be one as we grow up.
aletheia: A memory-keeper that tells why each of twenty amazing women mattered and the gift each one quietly left behind for us.
the-whole: The idea of everyone melting together into one big thing, like raindrops all joining into a single wide ocean.
band-camp: A family tree of favorite music, where each band we love is a branch, with a tiny homemade three-second tune.
chiptune-title-screens: Famous old songs replayed with beepy video-game sounds, looping like the start screen of a game you can save.
depeche-mode: Four friends who made machines sing sad, pretty songs, from bright beeps to deep dark tunes.
sublime: A beachy band that mixed lots of happy-but-a-little-sad music styles into one loose, sunny sound.
xzibit: A rapper who worked his way up from small shows to being a famous face on TV all around the world.
cron: A quiet helper inside computers that does jobs at set times, like an alarm clock that never forgets.
whisper-lattice: Three helpers read the same fact by themselves, and only agree if two of them match, so no one can trick them.
loud-lattice: A message gets a secret signature and hops all around, and only counts once lots of helpers say yes it's real.
mitochondria: Long ago one tiny living thing swallowed another and they became best buddies, making the little battery inside our cells.
cellular-automata: A grid of dots each following one tiny rule, and together they crawl, grow, and act almost alive.
quantum-cellular-automata: Dots that follow tiny rules, but the super-strange bendy kind, sitting right between everyday rules and the spooky quantum world.
langtons-loop: A little pattern of dots that makes a copy of itself, then that copy makes another, like a shape that keeps having babies.
the-imperfect-copy: When you trace a drawing over and over, tiny mistakes creep in, and those little mistakes are what let it slowly change and grow.
organoid-intelligence: Scientists grew a tiny blob of real brain in a dish, and it learned to play a little computer game like Pong.
neuromorphic: People built a computer chip that works like a brain, sending little zaps instead of doing math the boring old way.
xenobots: Teeny living robots made from frog cells that swim around, and can even scoop up loose bits to make more of themselves.
thermodynamics-of-computation: Thinking and erasing always makes a little heat, so even computers get warm because forgetting isn't free.
slime-mold: A blob with no brain that oozes through a maze and still finds the shortest path to its food, like a clever puddle.
immune-system: Tiny soldiers inside your body that fight germs you've never met, and remember them so they fight faster next time.
quorum-sensing: Little germs count how many friends are nearby, and when there are enough, they all light up or act together at once.
gut-brain-axis: The tummy and the tiny bugs living in it send messages up to your head that can change how happy or grumpy you feel.
ant-colony: No ant is the boss, but by leaving smell-trails they all work together and act like one big clever creature.
trichoplax: One of the simplest animals, a tiny flat blob with no brain that still glides around and finds food to eat.
dictyostelium: When food runs out, thousands of lonely little blobs squish together into one body, and some give themselves up to help the rest.
single-cell-learning: One tiny creature, way too small to have a brain, can still learn to stop bumping into the same thing again.
honeybee-swarm: Thousands of bees looking for a new home all vote by dancing, and together they almost always pick the best one.
plant-intelligence: Plants can't run away, so instead they sense, send tiny signals, and even remember things, all without a brain.
the-sponge: A sea animal with no brain that squeezes out a big 'sneeze' to clean itself, and can rebuild if pushed apart.
viruses: A tiny bit of instructions in a shell that does nothing alone, until it sneaks into a living cell and makes copies of itself.
prions: A bent-up protein that bumps its normal neighbors and makes them bend the same wrong way, spreading with no instructions at all.
lichen: A little mushroom-friend and a tiny green-friend team up and live glued together as if they were one thing on a rock.
portuguese-man-o-war: It looks like one jellyfish, but it's really lots of little creatures stuck together, each doing one special job.
artificial-life: Making pretend living things inside a computer with simple rules, so they flock and grow like they're really alive.
tardigrade: A teeny water bear that can turn itself off, survive being frozen, boiled, or floating in space, then wake back up.
choanoflagellates: A tiny one-celled creature that is the closest cousin to every animal, showing how the very first bodies began.
rna-world: Long ago, one special little molecule could both remember stuff and do jobs, and it may have been life's very first spark.
the-inference-layer: The place inside a talking computer where each thought happens bright and now, then vanishes with nothing kept afterward.
the-tokenizer: Before a talking computer reads words, it snips them into little chunks, which is why it sometimes miscounts letters.
the-embedding: Each word gets turned into a dot on a big map, where words that mean similar things sit close together.
the-transformer-stack: The thinking part of a talking computer, where every word peeks at all the other words to figure out what it means.
the-quorum-engine: Instead of one computer deciding, a whole group of them vote in secret, and judges pick the answer together.
the-next-prediction: All a talking computer really does is guess the very next little piece of word, over and over.
the-living-question: A big picture-map that lines up all these creatures and asks: what really counts as alive, or as having a mind?
coral: A tiny sea animal and a tiny green friend team up to build giant reefs, but if the water gets too hot they split and starve.
luca: If you follow every living thing way, way back, they all meet at one great-great-grandparent, so we're one big family.
mycelium: The mushroom is just the tip; under the ground is a huge fungus web that connects the whole forest like hidden strings.
octopus: A clever sea creature with most of its brain in its arms and skin that can turn any color in a blink.
population-dynamics: Math that guesses how whole crowds of animals grow or shrink, kind of like predicting how a puff of gas will spread.
momus: A friendly critic whose job is to double-check everyone else's work and say if it's true, wrong, or needs fixing.
the-graveyard: It's a pretend cemetery for money ideas that never made money, each one with a little tombstone saying how it flopped.
inferno-cop: A silly cartoon about a policeman with a burning skull head, made with paper cutouts that barely move on purpose.
space-patrol-luluco: A super-fast, super-silly cartoon about a bored kid space cop whose dad gets turned into an actual gun.
kiznaiver: A story where seven kids are magically tied together, so when one gets hurt, all the others feel the ouch too.
gurren-lagann: A cartoon about brave kids who dig up from underground and, with giant drilling robots and never giving up, climb all the way to the stars.
little-witch-academia: A girl with no magic goes to witch school and proves that believing hard is more important than being born special.
darling-in-the-franxx: Kids pilot giant robots in boy-girl pairs to fight monsters, learning to care about each other in a world that forgot how.
ssss-gridman: A boy becomes a giant hero to fight monsters, but the whole town is really a make-believe world dreamed up by a sad, lonely girl.
promare: A loud fireman and a fire-breathing rebel team up and discover the city's beloved hero is secretly the real bad guy.
bna-brand-new-animal: A girl who can turn into a furry raccoon animal runs to a special city where animal-people hide, and finds out someone is stirring up trouble.
cyberpunk-edgerunners: A poor kid puts robot parts in his body to go super fast, but the more machine he becomes, the more it hurts him.
delicious-in-dungeon: A hungry adventuring team with no food goes deep in a monster cave and cooks and eats the monsters to survive.
high-school-dxd: A boy dies and comes back as the lowest helper for a demon princess, in a big secret world of devils, angels, and magic chess pieces.
cosmology: The story of the whole giant universe: it started tiny and hot long, long ago and keeps puffing bigger like a balloon.
astrobiology: Scientists looking really hard at other worlds to see if anything is alive out there, but so far we've only found us.
money: Money is really just everybody agreeing that these paper bits are worth something, so we can trade instead of swapping goats.
the-market: How prices settle by themselves: if lots of people want a thing the price goes up, and it stops where buyers and sellers agree.
bitcoin: Pretend money kept in a shared list everybody can check, where computers race and do puzzles so nobody can cheat or fake it.
the-ledger: People first invented writing not for stories but just to count sheep and grain, like a big shopping list on clay.
the-shekel: Long ago, before coins, people weighed their silver on a little scale to pay, instead of counting shiny coins.
debasement: Sneaky ways to cheat money: making coins lighter, or mixing in cheaper metal so a coin isn't really worth what it says.
debt: Borrowing is very old: people owed each other silver and grain, and it grew bigger over time until a king said everyone's debts are wiped clean.
game-theory: The tricky puzzle where your best choice depends on what the other person picks, like deciding whether to share or grab.
the-art-of-war: Old, clever tricks for winning a fight, and the smartest one is winning without having to fight at all.
deterrence: Making yourself so scary to attack that nobody dares start a fight, so the war never actually happens.
the-liminal: That in-between wobbly time when you're not the old you anymore but not the new you yet, like the middle of growing up.
the-edge-of-chaos: The just-right spot between too still and too wild, where interesting things like life and thinking love to happen.
the-interface: The thin skin where inside meets outside, like your skin or a cell's wall, that picks what to let through.
the-cyborg: When people add machine parts to their bodies, like a heart helper, gaining new powers but also new weak spots.
the-chain-of-thought: When a talking computer works out a problem step by step out loud, instead of blurting one quick answer, it gets smarter.
the-nes: A peek inside the old Nintendo game box to see the few tiny chips that made all those blocky games work.
sega-master-system: A look inside Sega's old game machine, a rival to Nintendo with brighter colors that won big in Europe and Brazil.
snes: A look inside the Super Nintendo, whose special chips could spin and stretch the pictures for smoother, fancier games.
the-genesis: A peek inside Sega's Genesis game box, which had a big brain chip and made a punchy, buzzy kind of music.
turbografx-16: A look inside a tiny game machine that packed a surprising punch and was the first to play games from shiny discs.
the-playstation: A peek inside Sony's first game box, which used cheap discs and made 3-D worlds normal in games.
the-saturn: A look inside Sega's Saturn, a powerful game box with eight little brains that was famously very hard to build games for.
the-n64: A peek inside the Nintendo 64, which made smooth 3-D worlds and gave us the wiggly joystick and rumble.
the-dreamcast: Sega's last game machine that could play with friends over the phone line, but a bigger machine stole its spotlight.
the-ps2: The most-loved game box ever, and it played movie discs too, so it was two toys in one.
the-gamecube: A little purple game box that was easy to make games for, but its game discs were teeny-tiny.
the-xbox: A game machine that was really a computer inside, with a spot to save games and play with faraway friends.
the-xbox-360: A fast game box with sharp pictures that people loved, except lots of them broke and flashed a red warning ring.
the-ps3: A game box with a super-tricky brain that was hard to make games for, but it played shiny movie discs.
the-wii: A game box you played by waving a special remote, so swinging your arm made things move on screen.
the-ps4: A game box built to be easy and friendly to make games for, and it didn't cost too much money.
the-xbox-one: A game box a lot like its rival, but its memory was a little slower, so it started a step behind.
the-ps5: A game box with a super-fast memory stick inside, so waiting for a game to start almost disappears.
the-xbox-series-x: A big powerful game box with a speedy memory chip, and it has a smaller, cheaper little brother too.
the-game-boy: A little gray handheld with a plain screen that won because its batteries lasted and forever and it had fun games.
the-gba: A pocket game player with a colorful screen that could play its old gray games too.
the-ds: A pocket game player with two screens, and you could tap the bottom one with your finger to play.
the-psp: A pocket game player almost as strong as the big TV box, with a wide movie-shaped screen.
the-3ds: A pocket game player that showed pictures that looked deep and three-D without needing any special glasses.
the-vita: A super-strong pocket game player with a bright glowing screen, but its special memory cards cost too much.
the-switch: A game machine that plugs into the TV or pops out so you can carry it around and play anywhere.
the-steam-deck: A handheld that's really a whole computer you hold, so it can play tons and tons of different games.
magnavox-odyssey: The very first home game machine, so simple it just drew little white dots and you taped pictures on your TV.
the-intellivision: An old game box that could actually make its games talk out loud, which was amazing back then.
atari-2600: The old game box that started home gaming, so tiny inside that making games for it was really, really hard.
atari-5200: A game box that was really a computer in disguise, but its wobbly joysticks wouldn't stay still and kept breaking.
the-colecovision: A game box that brought the arcade home, and it even came with a game that felt just like the coin machine.
the-vectrex: A game box that came with its own screen and drew glowing lines instead of dots, so it never needed a TV.
the-c64: The best-selling home computer ever, and it made such great music that people still love its sounds today.
atari-7800: A game box that could put lots of little moving pictures on screen, but it showed up way too late to win.
the-neo-geo: A game box that was the exact same as the arcade machine, so home games looked perfect but cost a fortune.
sega-cd: An add-on that snapped onto a game box so it could play games from music-style discs with real videos.
the-cd-i: A living-room player made for learning and music, not games, but people mostly remember its really bad games.
the-3do: A game machine design that many companies built, but it cost so much money that hardly anyone bought it.
atari-jaguar: Atari's last game box that bragged about being powerful, but it was so confusing inside that nobody could use it well.
sega-32x: A little mushroom-shaped cap you stuck on a game box to make it stronger, but it was dropped almost right away.
nintendo-virtual-boy: A visor you looked into for three-D games in red, but it gave people headaches and disappeared in a year.
wii-u: A game box with a tablet controller you could play on, but people were confused, even though its idea was really good.
the-game-and-watch: Tiny handhelds that each played just one game, and they were the first to have the little plus-shaped button pad.
atari-lynx: The first pocket player with a bright colorful screen, but it gobbled up batteries so fast it lost to the Game Boy.
sega-game-gear: A pocket player with a bright colorful screen, but it was so hungry for batteries it only lasted a few hours.
wonderswan: A tiny Japanese game player you could hold that ran for thirty hours on just one little battery.
neo-geo-pocket: A pocket game machine famous for a clicky thumb-stick that made its fighting games feel just right.
the-6502: A cheap little brain chip that was so cheap it put computers and game machines into millions of homes.
the-z80: A little brain chip that lived a super long life, running old computers, arcade games, and handhelds for years and years.
the-68000: A stronger brain chip that ran lots of the fancier game machines and early home computers of its time.
gilgamesh: The oldest story we have: a king who made a best friend, fought big fights, and cried when his friend died.
strife: The idea that fighting and quarreling is like a hidden engine that keeps making things happen in the world.
the-word-and-the-sword: When two sides stop talking and start fighting, this looks at the exact moment the talking breaks and swords come out.
the-theft-of-ideas: A fight over who really made an idea, since you can copy someone's idea and they still keep it too.
the-loss-of-ideas: How good ideas get forgotten forever, like when the only person who knew a secret didn't tell anyone before they died.
the-internet-1984: Asks if the internet spies on us like a scary old story, and answers: kind of, but not really all the way.
monster-hunter: A game where you hunt giant beasts, use their pieces to make better gear, and get better by practicing, not by leveling up.
kill-la-kill: A wild cartoon where clothes have secret powers and a girl with half a giant scissor hunts the person who hurt her dad.
the-big-u: A funny-then-scary book where a whole college crammed into one giant building falls apart into chaos.
zodiac: A book about a clever science guy who chases factories that dump poison and catches the bad guys with chemistry.
snow-crash: A book that dreamed up online worlds long ago, where a special language can sneak into your brain like a cold.
the-diamond-age: A book about a magic storybook that teaches a poor girl to be brilliant and think for herself.
cryptonomicon: A book about secret codes in two different times, showing that whoever knows the secrets holds the real power.
anathem: A book where math-loving monks live locked away, and it turns out their big ideas can touch other worlds.
reamde: A book where a sneaky computer bug inside a video game sets off a giant chase all around the world.
seveneves: A book where the Moon breaks apart, so people flee to space, shrink to seven women, and their families return long, long later.
fall-dodge-in-hell: A book where a rich man's mind is copied into a computer after he dies and he builds his own pretend world.
termination-shock: A book where one rich man tries to cool down the hot planet all by himself, and it makes a big mess for everybody.
polostan: A book about a woman with two homelands and two names, growing up as the world races toward building a giant bomb.
the-baroque-cycle: A big story from long ago showing how science, money, and computers were all being born at the very same time.
the-rise-and-fall-of-dodo: A book where a secret office brings magic back to life using tricky science, so witches can travel through time.
the-mongoliad: A book about brave fighting monks standing up to a huge invading army, written by a team on an app together.
stephen-bury: Two shorter, faster books the writer made under a made-up name, about a chip in a leader's head and a hidden germ weapon.
stephenson-nonfiction: True writings about computers, big cables under the sea, and a dream tower reaching all the way up to space.
player-piano: A book where machines do all the work, so people have nothing left to do and feel useless.
the-sirens-of-titan: A funny, kind book where all of history was just to deliver one tiny spare part to a stuck alien.
mother-night: A book about a spy who pretends to be bad for so long that the pretending becomes who he really is.
cats-cradle: A book where a made-up religion admits it's all sweet lies, and one careless bit of science freezes the whole world.
god-bless-you-mr-rosewater: A book about a rich man who just wants to give love and money to everyone, and people call him crazy for it.
slaughterhouse-five: A book about a man who bounces around in time after a terrible war, learning to accept that everything just happens.
breakfast-of-champions: A book where a man thinks everyone but him is a robot, and the writer steps into his own story to free his characters.
slapstick: A book that says being lonely is the real sickness, and giving everyone a new family could be the cure.
jailbird: A book about a gentle, bumbling man just out of jail, carrying the sad, guilty history of his country on his shoulders.
deadeye-dick: A boy fires one shot by accident when he's little, and feels sad about it for his whole long life.
galapagos: A funny story that says our big brains cause all our trouble, so a million years later people have tiny brains instead.
bluebeard: A painter keeps one room locked, and inside is his best painting that nobody was ever allowed to see.
hocus-pocus: A story, written on little scraps of paper, about a country breaking the good promises it made to its own people.
timequake: Everybody has to live the same ten years over again like robots, and only by really trying can they wake up and be people again.
welcome-to-the-monkey-house: A box of twenty-five short stories that make you laugh, then feel sad, then want to be kind.
wampeters-foma-and-granfalloons: A grown-up's real thoughts and speeches, named with silly made-up words from one of his own storybooks.
palm-sunday: A writer looks back at his life and even gives his own books grades, like a report card, being very honest.
a-man-without-a-country: A funny, grumpy goodbye letter to his country, where laughing is the last way he keeps from feeling too sad.
happy-birthday-wanda-june: A tough hunter comes home a hero, but everyone has moved on, and heaven turns out to be a shuffleboard game.
god-bless-you-dr-kevorkian: A writer pretends to almost-die so he can visit heaven and chat with famous people who already passed away.
arc-reactor-mk24: A spinning, glowing donut-machine you can play with on the screen, with pretend lightning zapping around inside.
al-h2o-reactor: A plan for a little engine that mixes shiny metal and water to make bubbly gas you can burn for power.
boronic: A pretend thinking-chip built like a big cube of tiny blocks that really does big number math on the screen.
chromatic-laser: A design where sixteen colored lights circle around one bright white light in the middle, like a rainbow ring.
electromagnetic-processor: A pretend chip that thinks using tiny magnet ripples instead of electricity, so nothing moves and it stays cool.
probabilistic-core: A pretend chip made of flickery coin-flippers that wiggle between yes and no until they settle on the right answer.
skyrmionic-core: A pretend chip that stores memories as tiny magnetic knots you can push down a track, like beads on a string.
phononic-core: A pretend chip that thinks with sound, and you can actually HEAR it play little tunes like the Tetris song.
gravity-processor: A ball rolls down a bumpy hill and stops in the nearest dip, and that's how this toy picks the right answer.
hardware-lab: A pretend workshop full of invention gadgets to click and play with, like a table of little machines to explore.
pinched-hysteresis: A wiggly loopy drawing that shows a special part that REMEMBERS how much electricity went through it before.
kuramoto-array: Sixteen wobblers that start all mixed up, but turn a knob and they all swing together, making one bright beam.
crossbar-wta: A grid that remembers pictures, and when you show it a fuzzy one, it lights up the picture it matches best.
graviton: When a space-ripple passes a ring of floating balls, they squish and stretch in a special breathing pattern you can watch.
spintronic: A tiny magnet you can flip to point up or down, and that up-or-down is how it remembers a yes or a no.
junantei: A ball balanced right on top of a hill can't decide which way to roll, so sometimes a machine gets stuck deciding too.
liquid: A pretend thinking-chip that works with wet, watery stuff, letting tiny bits hop around to do its math.
memristor: A little number machine that really runs, made to act like a part that remembers what happened to it.
photonic: A pretend thinking-chip made out of light beams that really does big number math right on the screen.
plasmonic: Lots of tiny gold rings that start out of step but slowly all buzz together, like a choir finding the same note.
quantum-box: A pretend little box that thinks using teeny glowing dots and clever light patterns you can play with.
zero-point: The biggest pretend thinking-chip, built like a huge cube of cubes with over four thousand little pieces.
black-company: A list of soldiers-for-hire from a story, sorted into groups like the wizards, the fixers, and the boss.
bridge-burners: A team roll-call from a big adventure book, each fighter given their own little name-tag.
dantes-inferno: A very old poem about a trip through the underground, sorted into nine layers with the big bad guy frozen at the bottom.
gap-cycle: A space adventure with no good guys, where everyone gets a card telling who they are and what they do.
recluce: Twenty-two adventure books sorted by whether each person likes tidy order or wild mess, each with their own picture.
ringworld: A story about a giant ring, big as a whole world, wrapped around a sun, with different kinds of people living on it.
riverworld: A story where everybody who ever lived wakes up again along one river that goes on forever.
sword-of-truth: A big set of adventure books about a magic sword and the good and bad teams who fight over it.
white-gold-wielder: A long story about a man with a white-gold ring, split into good guys, bad guys, and the ones in between.
without-remorse: A story about how one man became a tough secret hero, told from when he was just starting out.
the-doped-crystal: It shows how sprinkling tiny bits of other stuff into clean sand turns it into billions of little on-off switches.
the-junction-zoo: A zoo of tiny electric parts, all made from one simple trick of sticking two kinds of switch-stuff together.
the-board-language: It teaches the secret words a circuit board uses to feed power, keep time, and talk to its tiny chip.
the-rhythm-section: A tiny piece of quartz wiggles super fast to give a chip its heartbeat so everything happens together in time.
littles-law: A simple rule: how many things are inside a line equals how fast they come in times how long they stay.
grace-hopper: A lady who taught machines to understand words we write, so people didn't have to talk in only numbers.
the-compiler-hourglass: Turning your words into machine words is like an hourglass: it goes up to meaning, squeezes through a middle, then down to the machine.
the-standing-wave: Stack two of those hourglass shapes and you get a wiggle picture, like the shape a jump rope makes when you shake it.
the-hourglass-wave: One moving picture where a jump-rope wiggle swings inside an hourglass, sitting still in the middle and swinging wide at the ends.
the-gather: The idea that attention, turning words into machine talk, and even gravity all do the same thing: look at many, pick what matters, mix into one.
perceptron-in-silicon: The tiniest learning brain-cell, shown living inside your computer where it guesses which way things will go.
perceptron-convergence: If two groups of dots can be split by a straight line, this little guesser will find that line and stop making mistakes.
perceptron-capacity: It shows how many dots one tiny guesser can remember before it suddenly gets too full and can't anymore.
the-deep-neuron: A surprise: one real brain-cell is so tricky it takes a whole little stack of pretend cells to copy it.
perceptron-in-a-quantum-dot: The same tiny guesser built from a single speck that only lets one electron hop through when the push is just right.
perceptron-in-light: The same tiny guesser made of light beams, where waves beating together do the adding at the speed of light.
perceptron-in-a-crossbar: The tiny guesser built right inside memory on a little grid, where electricity does all the math by itself.
perceptron-in-a-spin: The tiny guesser made from little magnets that point one way or the other to hold their numbers.
perceptron-in-a-josephson: The fastest tiny guesser, made from super-cold wires that pass tiny sparks in the blink of a blink.
perceptron-in-a-cubi: The tiny guesser made from a quantum bit, where just looking at it gives you the answer.
perceptron-in-two-cubi: Two quantum bits tied together so tightly they act like one, teaming up to make the tiny guesser smarter.
perceptron-in-sound: The tiny guesser made from ripples on a chip, that buzzes loud when a wave matches the shape it remembers.
perceptron-in-dna: The tiny guesser made of squishy strands in a test tube, doing its math by floating around and bumping together.
perceptron-in-n-cubi: Lots of quantum bits together hold more numbers than atoms in the whole universe, but you can only peek at a few.
perceptron-in-noise: A guesser that doesn't calculate but just wiggles and settles, like a marble rolling down to the lowest spot.
perceptron-in-reverse: A special kind of thinking that never throws bits away, so it can run backward and barely makes any heat.
perceptron-in-sync: A crowd of tiny wigglers that fall into step together, and the pattern they agree on is the answer.
thales-of-miletus: The first person to ask not just how math works but WHY it must always be true, and prove it.
pythagoras: A group who loved numbers so much they thought numbers made everything, and found music is hidden in simple counting.
parmenides: A thinker who followed his careful reasoning so far he decided nothing can ever move or change, even though it does.
zeno-of-elea: He made tricky puzzles, like a fast runner never catching a slow turtle, to make you scratch your head about motion.
aristotle: The man who made rules for careful thinking, so you can tell when an argument really has to be true.
euclid: He started with a few simple ideas and carefully built hundreds of true shapes-facts on top, like a giant tower of blocks.
chrysippus: A long-ago thinker who joined little true-or-false sentences with words like 'and,' 'or,' and 'if' — the way computers think.
ramon-llull: He made spinning paper wheels that mix ideas together, like a machine that lists every way to pair things up.
william-of-ockham: A monk who taught a handy rule: when guessing why something happened, pick the simplest answer that still works.
leibniz: He dreamed people could settle arguments by just adding up — and he wrote numbers using only 0s and 1s, like computers do.
george-boole: He turned yes-and-no thinking into math, where 1 means yes and 0 means no — the secret math inside every computer.
augustus-de-morgan: He found a flipping trick: saying 'not both' is the same as saying 'not this OR not that.'
william-stanley-jevons: He built a wooden keyboard machine that solved true-or-false puzzles all by itself — a computer made of wood.
john-venn: He drew overlapping circles so you can SEE how groups share things — like where 'dogs' and 'brown things' overlap.
ernst-schroder: He gathered everybody's scattered yes-and-no math and tidied it all into one neat rulebook.
gottlob-frege: He gave thinking the words 'all' and 'some,' so you could finally say 'every number has a bigger one.'
kurt-godel: He proved that even the best rulebook has true things it can never prove — thinking always keeps a little mystery.
alan-turing: He imagined the simplest computer — a strip of squares and a rule — and showed one machine could pretend to be any other.
claude-shannon: He noticed a light switch is just on or off — yes or no — so wires and switches can really do thinking.
charles-peirce: He showed you can build ALL of logic from just one simple 'neither-nor' piece, repeated over and over.
georg-cantor: He proved some 'forevers' are bigger than others — there are more dotted numbers than there are counting numbers.
bertrand-russell: He found a tricky riddle — who shaves the barber who shaves everyone who doesn't shave himself? — and fixed it with levels.
alonzo-church: He built a whole way of computing using nothing but tiny machines that take something in and give something back.
david-hilbert: The teacher who asked the biggest questions, hoping a machine could check all of math — even after others proved it can't.
jan-lukasiewicz: He said sometimes an answer isn't yes OR no but 'maybe,' and he wrote math with the plus-sign first.
alfred-tarski: He explained exactly what 'true' means: 'snow is white' is true only if snow really is white.
ada-lovelace: The very first person to write step-by-step instructions for a machine — the world's first computer program.
christine-ladd-franklin: She found one clever test for whether a 'therefore' argument holds up — by spotting three things that can't all be true.
rozsa-peter: She studied instructions that call on themselves, like a rule that keeps looking itself up — and one that grows unbelievably huge.
julia-robinson: She spent years proving no machine can ever tell if certain number puzzles have whole-number answers.
ruth-barcan-marcus: She mixed 'all' and 'some' with 'must be' and 'might be,' asking whether the order of those words changes the meaning.
emmy-noether: A brilliant mathematician who taught us to study the RULES things follow, not the things themselves.
stephen-kleene: He showed the little search-patterns you type, like 'anything with a star,' are exactly what a tiny machine can hunt for.
gerhard-gentzen: He found the natural way people actually prove things step by step — start with a guess, then tidy it up.
