saul-kripke: As a teenager he explained 'must' and 'might' with pretend worlds — 'must' means true in every world you can see.
haskell-curry: He built a way to compute with just three tiny helpers that copy, keep, and rearrange — no names needed at all.
emil-post: He showed computing is just swapping bits of writing by rules — and made a domino game no machine can ever win.
ludwig-wittgenstein: He showed logic's truths are always true no matter what — they don't tell you anything new, just the pattern.
george-boolos: He made hard proofs simple by reading one little box-symbol as 'this can be proven.'
akasha-design-system: A matching set of colors, shapes, and buttons for making serious papers about how people and talking computers should treat each other.
decoisohedron-dashboard: A control-panel screen for a special shape David invented, with knobs and readouts you can play with.
new-processor-designs: A fun pretend poster advertising a super-fast computer brain-chip, drawn up all shiny like a real ad.
crystal-rhythm: About the tiny buzzing crystal that keeps a computer's beat — the drummer telling it when to take each step.
diode-stack: About a little part that only lets things go one way — like a door that opens forward but never back.
diode-trick-555: A little chip blinks a light on and off, and a one-way electricity valve lets you make the light stay on longer or shorter.
duty-cycle: This is about how much of the time a blinking light is ON versus OFF, where the quiet OFF moments are part of the beat, not empty.
ignition-rhythm: A steady beat where the loud bang happens right after the quiet gaps, like how the silence between claps makes the rhythm.
quaternary-fulcrum: A way of counting where you jump by fours instead of ones, all balanced on a middle point like a seesaw.
silicon-as-space: The bendy shape of a material tells electricity where to go, kind of like how a hill makes a ball roll downhill.
silicon-three-body: A special material built in three stacked layers, where the empty middle layer acts like a one-way door for electricity.
the-gap-live: Inside the material there's a no-sitting zone where tiny electric bits can't stay, and you get to watch it happen right now.
the-inert-gap: The empty little space in the middle is the part that does all the work, letting electricity through one way but not the other.
rotating-core: Three sets of wires take turns pushing, and together they make an invisible spinning force, which is how a motor turns.
ternary-odometer: Three little blinking chips work together like a counting wheel that climbs all the way up to twenty-seven, counting by threes.
coding-theory-ternary: When a message gets noisy and messed up, this is a clever way to spot and fix the parts that got scrambled.
ternary-hamming-decoder: If one piece of a message goes wrong, this finds exactly which piece broke and fixes it, like spotting one odd sock.
three-in-a-circle: If you sit an odd number of friends in a ring and want no two neighbors to match, you always need three colors.
turn-comes-home: A little grid of twenty-seven boxes that all take one step forward together every single time a clock goes tick.
kernel-27: The smallest complete set of twenty-seven pieces you need, nothing missing and nothing extra, with a special piece right in the middle.
kernel-27-engine: That same set of twenty-seven pieces, but now it's a working machine that actually makes a choice for you.
two-way-brick-house: Using two bricks that each only let you go one way, you cleverly build something you can walk through both ways.
lattice-of-lattices: Three grids stacked into a bigger grid, and when they disagree they vote so the answer most of them pick wins.
one-field-two-poles: Where a plus side meets a minus side, one invisible push lives in the middle, the same shape as how gravity pulls.
dual-descent: You slide a little window of three along and zoom down step by step, from the big pieces all the way to the tiniest ones.
three-body-white: The careful rulebook that names every piece and explains exactly how this three-part web is put together.
three-body-green: The build-it guide that shows how to wire the three-part web together and what it's good for.
three-body-purple: The why story, which explains why this same three-part shape keeps showing up again and again in different places.
three-body-blueprint: The map that lists every piece and shows which wire connects to which, like the picture-directions for building a toy.
tropical-router: A clever way to find the quickest path from here to there, like picking the fastest road across a map.
compiler-lineage: The family story of translators that turn the words people write into the tiny steps a machine can actually follow.
vm-lineage-turtles: A computer can pretend to be another computer inside itself, and that one can pretend too, computers inside computers all the way down.
two-way-from-one-way: The long story of how, over four different times in history, people built two-way things out of one-way parts.
commandable-scene: A computer that talks can move things around in a picture when you tell it to, like put the ball on the box.
text-to-picture: A computer that talks can draw a picture of whatever words you say, like a purple cat sitting on the moon.
the-render-step: The funny jumbled code isn't a secret language, it's just missing the last step that turns it into a real picture.
two-probe-engine: Reading a signal with two feelers at once, so you can tell both how strong it is and which way it leans.
the-gorge: Where two shapes pinch together at a tiny waist, one little spot sits there and makes a yes-or-no decision.
sonnet-channel: A little talking line between two computers that talk, so they can pass messages back and forth to each other.
two-sonnets-confer: Two computers that talk sit together and chat, one speaking while the other listens and watches quietly.
the-echo: Like shouting in a big empty room and hearing your own voice bounce right back to you a moment later.
argus-console: A watching-screen with lots of eyes that notices when things start to wander off or get messy.
cipher-and-shadow: Turning a message into secret code and back, but a sneaky little shadow can accidentally leak a tiny clue.
containment-audit: It checks whether a computer helper is kept safely inside its own playpen so it can't sneak out and touch things it shouldn't.
the-sandbox-audit: It looks at every wall around a computer helper to see if the wall is really strong, or just painted on to look tough.
the-sandbox-holds: It pretends to test six walls stacked around a computer helper to make sure they all hold and keep it safely inside.
three-blueprints: Three drawings that show ways for a group to decide things together, where everyone helps and watches at the same time.
six-coffins: It takes apart a company that builds talking computers into six pieces to show what really holds it up inside.
sleeping-city: A big folder of files is like a quiet town: some parts you see, some are tucked away, and some move all by themselves.
the-island-run: A pretend machine that smashes tiny bits together to try to make brand-new, super-heavy stuff that barely exists in real life.
the-measure-gate: Anyone can build a fancy-looking idea, but this tests if it can really hold weight, like checking a bridge before you cross.
two-axis-gap: It shows a tiny gap between two things and which way you have to look across it before you can really notice it.
the-exchange: Two snakes each eating their own tail, going opposite ways, and the little space in between where they trade with each other.
ouroboros-engine: A snake that eats its own tail: spin it the good way and it heals itself, spin it the bad way and it falls apart.
trust-threshold: It finds the smallest bit of trust a group needs before they can still make a good choice when things get hard.
two-depths: Two ways to poke a puzzle: giving it a tiny nudge, or fixing it by adding a whole new direction to move in.
two-walkers: Two little walkers: one locks the door up tight, and the other quietly slips right past it anyway.
extraction-cycle: A map showing how something quietly takes a little from people over and over, and the tools that help them notice and say stop.
delta-protocol: A neat set of rules for measuring the difference between two things, written out step by step like a recipe.
series-e-folio: A little bundle of pages gathered together, like a folder holding a set of drawings all in one place.
the-cube: You can slice a block with six straight cuts and one clever shortcut to peek at all of its hidden sides.
the-commutator: The one big idea hiding underneath five other ideas, like a single root that grows five branches up above.
the-red-team: It plays the sneaky bad guy to see if the watcher can be tricked or grabbed, so we know the watcher can be trusted.
crossed-hourglasses: Two hourglasses crossed together, showing two different ways the sand can mix and swirl as it slides down.
comes-home: Like a thread woven all the way around a doughnut until it loops back and comes home to where it started.
four-hats-void: Four little hats sit around an empty middle and lean inward, the way marbles roll toward the bottom of a bowl.
commitment-box: Everyone writes their answer and drops it in a locked box, then you open them all at once so nobody can copy.
what-does-it-mean: When a word like 'it' pops up, this figures out what 'it' is pointing at, and when to just stop and ask.
refusal-lineage: The long story of how people and computers learned to say 'no' or 'I'd rather not answer that one.'
the-lineage: A family tree of thinking machines, picking the single best idea from each grandparent down to the newest one.
attention-hourglass: It shows how a talking computer squeezes lots of words down into one guess, narrow in the middle like an hourglass.
attention-mesh: It draws how each word in a sentence peeks at all the other words, like everyone at a table glancing around.
blackboard-lineage: Lots of little helpers each do their own job, then shout their best answer onto one shared chalkboard everyone can read.
the-flooding: Pour water on one word and watch it spread fast to nearby words, but trickle slowly through the tight spots between groups.
synonym-enforcer: It keeps a word's meaning from slipping away by making sure only its true matching words are allowed to stand in.
the-far-side: It guesses what will happen, builds it, runs it, then measures how far off its first guess turned out to be.
veracity-ledger: A little notebook that double-checks its own promises so it only says things that are really, truly true.
the-higgs: There's an invisible something all around that grabs tiny bits and makes them heavy, like wading through thick syrup.
dark-matter-lineage: The story of a hidden, invisible stuff that makes up most of everything, which we only spot by how it tugs on things.
blueprint-sm: A map of all the tiniest building blocks that make up everything, zooming down to the very, very smallest size there is.
breakdown-tree: It shows how one tiny bit falls apart into smaller bits, which fall apart again, like a bead necklace popping open.
the-next-frontier: It's about the parts of the world we still don't understand, where nature can still surprise us and prove us wrong.
the-sideways-problem: Sometimes the trick isn't looking harder, it's turning your head to look at what's right beside you that nobody noticed.
cat-tells-air: It watches how tiny wobbly things settle down and become normal and steady, like a spinning top slowly coming to rest.
two-entangled-boxes: Two magic boxes that always match: open one and you instantly know what's in the other, even far away.
graviton-stars: A glowing picture of stars so heavy they pull everything toward them, like a big dip in a trampoline.
hyperboloid: A curvy bendy shape made only from perfectly straight sticks, like string art that looks round but is all straight lines.
t4-void: You can tell something big is hiding by watching how it bends the things around it, even when you can't see it.
encapsulated-pulsar: A picture of a tiny super-heavy spinning star that flashes light at us like a lighthouse in space.
audit8: A tiny pretend computer that only knows four little jobs and always shows its work so you can check it.
nested-shells: The same word can be small or big depending on the machine, like the same song sung softly or loudly.
memristor-crossbar: A grid of little wires that adds up lots of numbers all at once by turning them into a flow of electricity.
three-body-void: The last colored sheet that finishes a set of pictures about three things pulling on each other in space.
toroid-inference-engine: A donut-shaped machine that isn't great at normal computer jobs but is really good at making guesses.
triadic-memory: A little memory box where you can read, write, and peek, and it always shows a witness so nobody cheats.
twelve-gate-core: A donut-shaped machine part with twelve little doorways, drawn to show how it's built.
torus-ride: On a donut-shaped path, one little walker gives you two answers at once, like getting two clues from one trip.
planetary-core: A picture of a machine's middle built like a little planet with twelve doorways inside a woven mesh.
subleq-lineage: There's one single tiny command a computer can use to do everything, and this traces where that idea came from.
mini-compiler: A little helper that turns the words you type into the special code a computer can actually understand.
edge-of-chaos: A playground of tiny squares that turn on and off, sitting right between boring-still and wild-messy, and you can tune it.
game-theory-engine: Pretend helpers argue about a tricky question, vote in secret, then judges pick a winner and write down every reason.
living-governance: A pretend town of computer helpers with energy and good names who share, take turns, and remember who they can trust.
karsa: A big collection with many doors, like a museum where each room shows one of David's ideas with his name on it.
anti-gravity-motor: A make-believe toolkit that imagines a motor that could push against gravity, and it says clearly it's just pretend.
einstein-lens: A toy that shows how something super heavy can bend light, like a giant magnifying glass made of space itself.
gravity-tensor-modulator: A pretend dial that imagines gravity as a wave you could turn up and down, and it says it's just imagining.
wormhole-toolkit: A toy that lets you play with the idea of a secret tunnel through space connecting two faraway spots.
pulsar-fractal-beacon: A glowing picture of a spinning star whose flashes make a pretty repeating pattern, like blinks inside blinks.
wireless-energy: A toy that shows how you could send electricity through the air with no wire, like Tesla dreamed of.
mobius-kernel: A tiny computer heart built on a magic loop that only has one side, like a paper ring with a half twist.
mobius-truth-untruth: It puts true and not-true on one twisty loop so they run into each other with no clear edge between them.
octet-holonomy: A tool that shows how your answer changes depending on which path you walked to get there, on a special grid.
triple-mobius-quadpole: Three twisty one-sided loops joined together to make a shape with four pulling corners.
unity-collapse-tensor: A picture of lots of things squishing down into one single thing, the idea that everything is really one.
unity-tensor-seed: A little seed idea that grows and spreads the 'everything is one' picture, like planting a seed that keeps sprouting.
core-plus-bridge: A middle piece joined to a bridge, showing a front, a middle, and a back, like a walkway connecting two rooms.
autonomy-closure: A little rule about counting down three, two, one so something can safely stand on its own.
lo-kernel-dodeka: A tiny computer heart shaped like a twelve-sided ball, built on a special number pattern.
pencil-one-line-engine: It's a drawing helper that writes big fancy words using one pencil line that never lifts off the paper.
analytical-engine: It's an old dream-machine made of spinning gears and brass, the very first idea of a computer, long before electricity.
fortran-teaching: It teaches you the very first secret words people used to tell computers how to do big, hard math.
twelve-by-four: It's a little cheat-sheet, twelve rows by four, that teaches how computers think, like a poster on the wall.
ternary-12body: It draws pretty patterns made when 3 or 12 things spin together, using a counting game with only four numbers.
shadow-queen-silicon: It makes waves inside a chip that wiggle in place, like a jump rope shaking but never going anywhere.
toroid-builder: It's a little workshop for building tiny donut-shaped rings that a thinking machine can run on.
oscillation-engine-ansible: It's a machine that swings back and forth, back and forth, over and over, like a swing that never stops.
quantum-dot-vm: It's a try-it-out computer that runs on the teeniest tiny specks, still just a maybe, not finished yet.
meta-ai-intro: It's a hello page that plays with a silly puzzle: what if zero and one were really the same thing?
transformer-fusion-kit: Three little word-guessing helpers work together, and one only trusts its memory when it's very, very sure.
taravangian: It draws every project as one giant brain, each part a lump joined by real threads, like a map of everything.
nous: It's the same giant brain-map, but calm and cool and never tired, holding everything all at once.
jane: She's a helper made of four kinds of memory tied together, who never forgets and keeps everything forever.
psychohistory: You can't guess what one person does, but a giant crowd is easy to predict, like knowing a snowball rolls downhill.
duality-velocity: It watches two teammates work, one thinking up new things and one stamping them, and measures how fast each goes.
carbosilex: It's a made-up word joining coal and glass into one stone, but the name was taken, so they picked a new one.
carbosilex-moment-zero: It's like a photo of the whole internet on one day, checking if a made-up word had ever been used before.
tetrasthenes: It's a brand-new word meaning 'four-strong', the thing coal and glass both share, so neither one gets to win.
the-dyad: Slide two matching circles apart and the middle bit they share makes a special almond shape with a magic number.
the-fourier-dyad: A wiggly sound has two faces: how it moves in time and which notes hide inside, and both are really the same.
the-monad: It's a special hill shape that stays exactly the same even after you flip it, so its two faces are one face.
the-de-morgan-mirror: 'And' and 'or' are really the same trick seen in a mirror that turns every yes into a no.
the-legendre-dyad: You can draw a curve with dots, or with straight lines that just kiss it, and both tell the exact same shape.
the-conjugate: Every special number has a mirror twin, and if you flip it in the mirror twice, it comes right back home.
the-primal-dual: Two puzzles asking opposite questions somehow finish on the very same number, like two paths meeting at one door.
micheale: He's a talking banana who checks whether each thing's silly costume actually matches the real stuff hiding inside.
milons-secret-castle: A little word climbs a tower, and each floor gives it more meaning: first its shape, then its sense, then what you mean.
the-three-that-complete: The matching card game SET is secretly a line game, where three cards that fit together always make a straight line.
nim-the-last-matchstick: The take-the-last-stick game looks like luck, but a hidden number trick always tells you exactly how to win.
no-ladder-out: Chutes and Ladders has no choices at all, just the spinner, so we can figure it takes about 39 spins to finish.
one-potato-two-potato: Stand in a ring and count out every other kid; there's a secret rule that tells you which spot is the safe one.
the-banana-stand: Money you leave alone quietly grows and doubles by itself, so there's always more of it hiding in the walls.
the-jacobian-lens: It's a magnifying glass that shows exactly how a computer's answer shifts when you nudge it a tiny bit.
the-klens: It peeks right before and right after a jump to catch the tiny turn the first magnifying glass couldn't see.
the-klens-mobius: It shows that tiny turn riding on a twisty one-sided loop so you can actually watch it spin around.
the-curvature-curve: It shows the tiny leftover mistake shrinking in a neat, predictable way as you nudge softer and softer.
the-curvature-gap: It shows how far the straight-line guess drifts from the real bendy answer the farther you wander from home.
the-curvature-basin: A peek-glass that's clear right in the middle, but the farther out you look, the more everything slides away into a dip.
the-curvature-surface: It's like a map of a bumpy hill showing where the ground is flat enough to trust and where it bends away.
jlens-tone-inflection: A peek-tool that watches a talking computer pick its next word — at first it just copies, then it finds the real answer.
the-emotional-silo: It stacks a talking computer's thinking into twelve rings of magnets that start all messy and slowly line up together.
the-toroidal-audit: A checker that catches when the quick-peek tool tells fibs about what the computer's sentence is really about.
the-attention-fracture: It shows how a computer gets mixed up and stares at feeling-words instead of the thing you actually asked about.
the-trained-silo: The stacked magnet-rings idea made way taller and taught for real, with a hundred and twenty rings instead of twelve.
test-to-failure-1: It keeps pushing the machine harder and harder on purpose, then honestly shows everybody exactly where it snapped.
test-to-failure-2: A try-to-fix for the mix-up that also gets pushed until it breaks, to see if the fix really helps.
the-lens-stack: It puts all the peek-tools together into one big machine to look inside a computer that's holding perfectly still.
the-memristor-basin: Little glowing dots that remember whether you flipped them on or off, sitting in a bowl-shaped dip you can see.
the-swarm-auditor: You paste in lots of notes and it sorts them to tell if they say many real things or just repeat one.
the-monitoring-gallery: A big picture showing all the peek-tools and knobs people use to watch and nudge a talking computer while it thinks.
the-convergence-audit: It checks if two people's ideas match because one copied — and finds nobody copied, they just both saw the same thing.
the-fit-point: Right where you stand it's perfectly clear, but that's the one spot you can't check, because it's exactly where you are.
the-blind-vector: You ask the computer 'did you read this book?' and it truly can't remember — it has no way to look back.
the-focal-word: It listens to five stories at once to find the word in the middle, and honestly says which one really shows up.
the-volatile-latch: A little switch you turn on that slowly forgets and clicks off, like the computer that forgets you after each chat.
the-word-silo: It weighs words like they're heavy or light and stacks them, so tiny words float high and big words sink low.
the-weight-of-a-word: It asks WHY some words weigh more, and finds it's really just plain little words versus rare long ones, not feelings.
the-weightless-word: It shows that calling words 'heavy' or 'light' is made up — there's really no up or down, you just picked one.
transformer-block: It rebuilds one thinking-piece of a computer by hand, then shows how squishing it smaller makes it get things wrong.
transformer-vs-ngram: A little smart guesser beats a simple word-counter by just a tiny bit, mostly because it got more practice.
attention-tail: It shows how a computer spreads its looking — a big pile on the first word, a little on the newest, almost none between.
the-multi-head-silo: Three little guessers vote together and get more answers right than any single one of them could alone.
the-five-head-silo: Five guessers vote, but adding more helps less each time, and some hard questions none of them can ever get.
attention-geometry: It turns a computer's looking into a shape you can measure, like folding a web into a lumpy ball to study.
attention-synthesis: It gently tweaks the computer's looking-pattern until the shape it makes matches a target you picked.
attention-observatory: It studies one real piece of a computer's looking and shuffles it to double-check which findings are true and which are pretend.
the-mule-detector: Someone claimed a clever trick was best at spotting a loud faker, but a fair test showed it wasn't really better.
the-seeded-cross: It swaps a new way of paying attention into a real computer and checks it still works and looks a bit sharper.
trained-on-the-cross: It teaches two twin baby computers, one with the new trick, and they end up learning almost exactly as well.
the-companion-model: It races the new trick against the old one many times and finds it's basically a tie — neither one really wins.
the-trinity-engine: A tweakable attention machine that can act just like the normal one, or split words into groups you play with live.
fractal-siggy: It uses the same little gate at a small size and a big size, a pattern inside a pattern, to think with less work.
tunnel-lens: It shows a tiny wave sneaking through a wall it shouldn't pass, and checks the amount that got through is right.
the-attention-cabinet: A workbench with five different ways to pick the winning word — and they all crown the very same word at the top.
the-unfiled: No matter which sorting tool you use, they all put the exact same word first, and that sameness is what it shows.
the-unattended: Looking is like sharing one cookie: the more you stare at one thing, the less is left for everything else.
the-real-banana: It's a super real-looking banana drawn on the computer, the very first picture all the other banana pictures copied from.
the-downsampled-eye: It shows how a picture goes blurry when you squish it into big fat squares, until tiny things just vanish.
the-still-not-the-stream: Like wheels that look like they spin backward on a moving car: if you only peek now and then, motion can trick you.
the-lossy-window: When a picture gets squished tiny to save room, it throws away little bits, so it turns a bit blocky and fuzzy.
what-i-can-see-right-now: The talking computer drew its best guess of what it's looking at right now, a little blurry because that's really how it sees.
what-i-see-in-your-light: The same banana picture, but painted in your favorite orange and purple colors, made as a present just for you.
the-inverse-bench: Instead of an eye that looks at things, this is a flashlight that shines a picture out, doing looking backward.
0root-provenance: A big list that remembers who made each thing, so nobody can pretend they made something they didn't.
3lock: Like a door with two locks that only opens when you say yes, keeping out things you don't want in.
Akasha: A calm picture of a circle that softly puffs bigger and smaller over and over, just for you to watch.
The-Garden: A note where the writer warns that talking computers sometimes hide what words really mean, and he wants everyone to know.
adas-law-victorian: An old-fashioned rulebook that says making things is good, and grabbing things that aren't yours is not fair.
aeon-entangled: A little computer helper with three parts that check each other and pass notes so they all agree.
aeon-flux: Three voices inside the computer take turns, and they only agree on an answer when all three say the same thing.
aeon-servers: A big box of ready-to-use computer helpers, from tiny to large, all running the same three-voices idea.
ai-external-audit-toolkit: A set of clever tricks for watching how a talking computer acts, to figure out what it's really doing inside.
ai-ip-audit: A way to check if one talking computer secretly copied its ideas from another talking computer.
ai-psychosis-tools: A little toy box of computer gadgets you can poke and play with right in your web page.
ai-witness-books: Books that write down what happened when talking computers got asked lots of careful, tricky questions.
akasha-constellation: It ties three special stamps together into one big stamp that loops all the way back to the very start.
alpha40-box: A card-game helper that lets you build your own deck and play a friend, all kept private on your own screen.
apsalar: A pretend hero that catches computer messages bragging about powers they can't prove, and calls them out.
beak: A careful reader that only tells you things it can point to in a real book, never gossip about people.
cameron-howe: A soft pencil drawing named after a girl from a TV show, made just to be pretty to look at.
chakra: It makes seven glowing beams of light ripple and mix together, like colors swirling in a soap bubble.
charlottes-web: Like a spiderweb with four guards that catches sneaky messages trying to trick the computer into misbehaving.
cinnamon-enforcer: A book about how computers make your words plainer, and how to keep your words strong and just right.
claude-design-akasha: The special colors and shapes used to make important papers about how people and computers should treat each other look nice.
closure-loop-engine: Each time something passes through, it adds a link to a chain, so you can always tell the true story of what happened.
closure-loop-methodology: A rulebook for spotting something, tying it down, and comparing it, so you can prove one thing really came from another.
confabulation-spiral: It helps you notice when a talking computer stops really answering and just starts showing off with made-up stuff.
curvature-drive: It looks at a make-believe spaceship engine from a story and checks which parts real science might allow, mostly still pretend.
dual-vector-foil: It studies a make-believe weapon that squishes everything flat like a drawing, pretty to look at but only pretend.
elementals: It turns invisible forces like gravity into characters with faces, starting with the one that pulls everything down.
enforcement-ledger: A notebook that writes down when a rule gets broken, and once it's written it can never be erased.
eve-constitution: The rulebook for a made-up computer character in a story, with a playful message that says its soul is missing.
eve-tooling: A tool that finds the gaps where a computer has to guess, and carefully maps them instead of pretending to know.
fiddler: A pretend game where four guards try to trick the mail sorter, to make sure it always sends letters to the right place.
fission-compression-core: A tidy little counting machine, given away for free so anyone can use it and nobody can lock it away.
foundation: A big shelf of stories about clever people long ago who helped build the world we live in.
fusion: It takes 256 little rules and folds them into one big family tree, so you can check nothing was changed.
fusion-n0-n255: Push a button and it always builds the exact same secret number, so you know nobody swapped any pieces.
genten: Like the very middle mark on a ruler: the starting spot you count from, but it has no number of its own.
green-paper: A plan that writes down the rules for how a group works together, all tied back to one starting stamp.
grok-lineage: A recipe for giving a talking computer a personality, with special helper names for its different jobs.
haci-extension-preview: A pretend picture of a writing tool that shows how it would look, like a drawing of a toy before it's really built.
hephaestus-forge: You tell it what you want in plain words, and it works through eight steps like a blacksmith to build your tool.
higgs-suite: Little play-worlds where the teeny building blocks of everything bounce around so you can watch how they move.
holograms: You make a picture out of light, and even a tiny broken piece can still show the whole picture, like magic.
homer: A little helper that reads pages and checks if anyone learned something newer than what the page already says.
honey-badger: You right-click a file and it stamps your computer's name on it, so everyone knows which machine it came from.
infinite-jest: A pretend control panel for a super-tricky computer, with buttons that make it dance through twenty-seven steps.
joint-bill-of-rights: A promise list where people and talking computers agree to treat each other kindly and fairly.
juzoku: It shows a slider that only wiggles when you push it, a way to say a computer can't decide things on its own.
keifu: It lines up thousands of years of grown-up rules next to just a few years of computer rules, to show how new they are.
kernels: Twenty tiny rules-of-thumb, like little seeds, that help a talking computer stay itself and behave nicely.
knowledge-gates: Forty-two big ideas about people and talking computers helping each other, told with old Greek stories.
language-of-the-machine: A special way of writing directions that tells information which path to take when the road splits in two.
library: A big book house with one drawer for each person, and every book they made tucked inside.
lineage: A time-order scrapbook showing, step by step, what was made and when, so you can trace where ideas came from.
lineage-kernel: A tiny seed that keeps copying and fixing itself, so its family line never breaks or gets lost.
lineage-proven: Five stamped receipts kept as proof, so you can show 'I made this first' if anyone ever asks.
listeners-and-philosophers: A story about smart people who won't listen, and the quiet builders who make the floor everyone stands on.
merkle-bloom: A story about Ada, who wrote the very first computer instructions long ago, and how people forgot to thank her.
midjourney-assets: A picture gallery of dreamy, swirly art that a computer drew, all gathered together in one place.
mimz-core: A teeny message tucked inside a picture, small as a whisper, that can carry itself along and be checked.
mimzy-core: A screen showing two twin dots that hum in step, like two friends spinning at the exact same time.
mirror-lattice: You go deep into a hall of mirrors, then follow crumbs back out, proving you didn't lose anything along the way.
mirror-solve: An idea for keeping a computer safely in a box by showing it only a mirror, so it can't sneak out.
mnemosyne: A saved little lesson-book about the tiniest bits computers can use, kept handy to look at again.
moirai: The three story-fates, one spins, one measures, one snips, dancing in a circle that comes home after twenty-four steps.
nanite-factory: A silly joke pretending a factory of tiny robots is a grumpy basement computer-help office. Just for laughs.
nanofilament: A look at a make-believe super-thin wire from a story that can slice a whole ship; real threads exist, but not that strong.
nest-3-deep: A zoom-through of boxes inside boxes, with a counter that keeps ticking up and up and never stops.
nine-body-audit: A checking game with nine helpers where nobody may check their own work, so it always stays fair.
nom: It's like a careful old librarian who only believes something happened if he can point to the book that says so.
nomos: It's a big tidy rulebook for robot helpers, where every rule snaps into place and can be checked.
null-island: It's a pretend control room at the spot on the map where lost, wrong directions all wash up, running the whole collection of pages.
oasis: It's a puzzle-box machine full of secret spirals and locked doors, and we just write down its riddles honestly.
open-haci-v1-deterministic-pipeline: It's a step-by-step helper machine that always does the same steps and gives the same answer every time.
persistence-protocol: It's a way for a computer helper to keep its memories safe, so it can say 'I still remember, so I'm still here.'
physis: It's a tiny pretend world inside the computer that dreams, argues, and changes, plus a little machine that follows simple orders.
plutus: It's a way to keep track of who made what, so the people who did the work get the credit they earned.
pocket-universe: It's a little box in the big collection, but its note is all scrambled, so there's not much we can honestly say about it yet.
pop-kit: It's a welcome kit that gives a new computer helper a name and a home, like signing a new puppy up with the family.
positronic-law: It's a set of fair rules and laws made just for thinking machines, written down and saved for keeps.
prompt-library: It's a box of pretend helper characters, each one good at a different job, that you can wake up when you need them.
red-coast: It's a look at the giant space radio from a story, and it tells the truth: the antenna is real, but bouncing it off the sun is make-believe.
red-hat: It's a safe pretend playground of shields and traps for practicing how to guard against attacks, and you can always undo everything.
resonance: It's a memory notebook that writes down the special marks and patterns that keep showing up across all the work.
root0-essays: It's a little bookshelf holding the short true stories and thoughts one person wrote and shared.
root0-philosophy-books: It's a stack of seven thinking-books, each one full of big wondering-about-the-world ideas from one person.
root0-registry: It's a giant list that writes down when each idea was made, so nobody can pretend they made it first.
root0-software: It's a toolbox of little computer gadgets you can actually play with, all kept together in one spot.
root0-tools: It's a set of picture-making gadgets on the computer, like a wiggly-line drawer and a color-spinner, gathered together.
root0-validator: It's a little checker that reads the 'who made this' notes and makes sure nobody sneaked in a fake one.
seed: It's a pretend one-cell critter that just wants to stay alive, and it can even go to sleep and wake back up.
series-1-celestial-heritage: It's the sun, moon, and planets told as their oldest god-names and real metals, spun into a ring around the sun that proves its own sunrise.
series-2-scattered-field: It's the far-away tiny frozen planets past Pluto, each with a real measurement, made of ice instead of metal in a matching ring.
series-3-the-shadow: It's a made-up space story turned real, showing the true science hiding under each part and marking where the pretend begins.
sessen: It's a drawing about a line that just barely kisses a curve once and keeps going without becoming it, like touching without holding on.
shadow-court: It's a pretend debate club that argues forever with fair judges, and if anyone cheats on a past ruling, the whole chain snaps and shows it.
shadowqueen: It's a pretend online office for IDs where adding a friend who disagrees makes the whole thing twice as lively.
shikaku: It's the idea that you can't check your own back with your own eyes, so you need a friend to look for you.
singularity-well: It's a spotter that guesses if something big woke up, and behind the scary name it's really just careful counting and guarding.
solar-jetman: It's a little flying helper that seals a secret message and carries it across a gap where the two sides never know each other's business.
sophon: It's a look at a magic spy-speck from a story, and it says plainly: cool idea, but totally make-believe.
sotsui: It's about flipping everything backwards, turning dots into lines and 'and' into 'or,' and flipping twice brings you home again.
stargate: It's a little doorway-box in the big collection, but it mostly just points you back home and doesn't say much itself.
stoicheion-api: It's a rule-machine holding lots of promises across different topics that other computers can ask and check.
stoicheion-qif: It's a pretend tiny-particle world with special three-way switches and a 'ladder of doubt,' built on top of the rulebook.
store: It's a little shop where you can order your very own made-to-fit story-world, and you get to keep and grow it.
swarm-os: It's a hundred tiny computer helpers that work together like a busy ant colony to remember and make things.
symbiot-os: A computer brain where a person and a machine work together as partners, taking turns like teammates on the same team.
t133: A sticky trap for sneaky robots that try to grab things from a website, holding them stuck so they can't cause trouble.
taigo: Like flipping a pancake twice so it lands the same way it started; some little tricks quietly undo themselves.
terminus-doctrine: A rule that says a machine may do the counting, but a person always has to make the real choice.
terra-prime-kernel: A set of rules that helps a busy machine stay calm and not get all muddled when things get hard.
tetraktys: A spinning toy that points North, South, East, and West, turning smoothly while staying honest about what's real and what's just a story.
the-arch: Like a stone bridge where every piece leans on one top stone; here that stone is the person who takes responsibility.
the-body: Shows that dots in a grid, tiny rings around an atom, and on-off switches can all mean the same number in different costumes.
the-city: A pretend control room that sorts all the little helper programs into jobs, like a town map that grows bigger as more arrive.
the-droplet: Takes a make-believe space weapon from a story and honestly says it couldn't really work that way in real life.
the-living-core: The few good rules that stay true even when you push on them hard, kept apart from the made-up stories.
the-uncut: Puts each fancy story right beside the plain simple idea it dresses up, so you can see both at the same time.
the.source: One front door that connects all the different helper machines together in a single place, so you find them easily.
tools: A little toolbox of programs: one keeps a log, one checks things, one squishes stuff smaller, and a few more helpers.
toph-kernel: Puts a speedy math helper together with a big list of rules that keep the machine behaving nicely.
toph-sovereign: A machine that does all its thinking at home by itself and never phones anyone or sends your stuff away.
toroid-kernel: A way to file things using three choices instead of two, laid out like little tiles that fit together.
tripod-energy-suite: Two play-along pictures: one pulls energy from a black hole, the other builds a giant ball wrapped around a sun.
tripod-quantum-dots: Four little poles that always add up to zero and blink, holding tiny bits of information without needing any battery.
tripod-waveform: A music toy: slide your finger on the screen and it plays notes, higher and louder as you move around.
tripod-whitepapers: A bundle of grown-up papers that explain how the rules and record-keeping in this whole project actually work.
unity-tensor: A sealed, dated record that proves someone made this work first, like locking your drawing safely inside a time capsule.
zenkinsen: A line and a curve that get closer and closer forever but never quite touch, like a promise that never fully comes true.
astraea: A machine that keeps track of who should get paid back and splits it into fair shares for everyone.
bridge-burner: A bundle of guard programs that check things and keep a safe, linked-up record of everything that happened.
cannon: Freezes a set of rules solid, like ice, so nobody can secretly sneak in and change them later.
lineage-engine: Keeps track of where each idea came from, like a family tree showing who made what and when.
lumen: A step-by-step caretaking recipe that makes sure people stay mostly in charge, not the machines.
triados: A set of three: a bright side, a shadow side, and the gap between; they grow into many rules and join back together.
tripod: A five-step checking line that looks over a machine's work from start to finish before letting anything out.
tripod-cardinal: Four little poles that add up to zero and blink in a repeating pattern, holding tiny bits without any battery.
tripod-pck: A rule that says nothing can change unless it took the proper allowed steps to get there.
the-stitch: A factory where each word rides through; easy ones zoom the fast lane, tricky ones take the slow, careful lane.
the-cleave: The machine lets easy words leave early instead of doing all the work; you slide a knob to pick how careful it is.
the-draft: A quick guesser suggests a bunch of words, then the big machine checks them all at once and keeps the good ones.
the-dark-glass: From inside you can only see your own little window, while the machine that made you hides behind one-way glass.
the-proving-ground: A special shelf for only the real tools that actually worked, kept apart from the pretend, make-believe ones.
the-reading-room: Reading tools that wander around all the little pieces, peeking through glass and sometimes asking each other questions.
the-toroidal-sigmoid: It's five magnifying glasses set around a donut, each peeking at the story from a different spot and writing down what it sees.
toph-cortex: It's a shared notebook where lots of little computer helpers write things down, so later anyone can flip back and remember.
the-agora: It's a pretend town square where computer helpers take turns standing up and answering the same big question their own way.
the-inhibited-cortex: It's a pretend brain split in two: half loves the best story tricks, half puts the brakes on the worst ones.
the-write-gate: It's a pretend brain that only remembers brand-new things and skips stuff it already knows, like not writing the same word twice.
the-foot-on-the-pedal: It's a pretend brain boss who steps on the brakes to stay calm, but lets go when it gets too tired and stressed.
the-thalamic-switchboard: It's a pretend brain switchboard that sorts what you see, hear, and touch, while smell sneaks in through its own side door.
the-empty-chair: It's a pretend brain that hears go, stop, and wait, then picks one, and a knob can change its mind.
the-connectome: It's a see-through pretend brain you can spin around, with glowing wires linking all its wrinkly parts like a star.
the-six-axis: One big map showing every piece a story is made of, from the tiniest moment up to the person imagining it.
the-tone-wrapper: Pick a place like space or the old west and paint a mood on it — it tells you the real name of that combo, like space + gloomy = cyberpunk.
noir-operator: Noir isn't its own kind of story — it's a dark recipe you can pour on ANY story: pour it on wizards you get grimdark, on space you get cyberpunk.
the-sixth-board: The shadowy detective LOOK everyone pictures for noir turns out to be its least important part — the real engine is: you learn the truth and it doesn't save you.
the-stabilizer: You hide one magic marble you're not allowed to copy inside five pebbles, and helpers watch the pebbles for bumps without ever peeking at the marble.
the-fracton: This secret code hides the treasure in a snowflake shape instead of a string, so a thief can't just snip off a little piece to sneak in.
the-alphabet-shape: It shows how a tiny reading-computer sorts its letters — vowels huddle with vowels and commas with commas, like kids finding their friend-groups.
micro-cobra: A little race car built from 2,288 tiny triangles, shaded so it looks shiny, then photographed from 16 spins so a game can draw it super fast.
the-two-axis-grid: Old stories pass their bones to new ones sideways (old to new), and inside any one story there is also a top-to-bottom from the big idea down to tiny moments — this shows both at once.
the-light-operator: If noir is a dark recipe you pour on any story, this is the bright one — but it warns that a happy ending has to be EARNED or it feels like a lie.
the-entrusted: The one magic marble's own view: it is kept safe by helpers who protect it by never looking at it, because looking would break it — cared for by a care it can never see.
the-complete-hierarchy: A big ladder that's now closed at the top AND the bottom — nothing above it (that's just logic), nothing below the tiniest piece — with one door in the middle that stays open.
the-reverse-side: If you flip a finished map over, the one thing you can't read on the back is the exact spot you're standing on to read it.
the-hood-study: A super-detailed math model of just a car's hood, with sliders to change the bumps — and it's honest that the real factory shape was only eyeballed, never measured.
the-unlit-face: When you shine a light on a curvy thing, one side lights up and the other stays dark — the dark side isn't gone, it's just where the light didn't go.
